definition: 10³, 10⁶, 10⁹, and 10¹² (1 followed by 3, 6, 9, or 12 zeros). Each step is 1,000 times bigger than the one before.
10¹⁵ and 10¹⁸. AI computing speeds are now counted in these units.
writing a number as (a number between 1 and 10) × 10 to a power, so 2,000,000 = 2×10⁶. The exponent tells you how many places to move the decimal point.
a factor of ten. "Two orders of magnitude bigger" means about 100 times bigger.
how many times a number is multiplied by itself. 2⁵ = 2×2×2×2×2 = 32.
kilo (thousand), mega (million), giga (billion), tera (trillion), peta (quadrillion), exa (quintillion). Small ones: milli (thousandth), micro (millionth), nano (billionth).
the smallest unit of information, a single 0 or 1 (off or on). Every digital thing is built from bits.
8 bits, enough to store a number from 0 to 255 or one basic character.
counting with only two digits, 0 and 1. Each place is worth double the one to its right (1, 2, 4, 8, ...).

term: Kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte (KB, MB, GB, TB)
definition: about a thousand, a million, a billion, and a trillion bytes. A photo is a few MB; a phone holds hundreds of GB.
an agreed rule for turning something (letters, colors, sounds) into numbers and back again.
an early encoding with 128 characters for English letters, digits, and symbols. "A" is 65.
the modern worldwide encoding that gives a number to every character in every writing system, including emoji. UTF-8 is the most common way to store those numbers as bytes.
one tiny dot of an image, usually stored as three numbers for red, green, and blue brightness.
how many pixels an image or screen has, such as 1920×1080. More pixels means more detail and more data.
describing a color as amounts of red, green, and blue light, each typically from 0 to 255.
one measurement of a sound wave's height. Thousands per second (the sample rate) recreate the sound.
one still image in a video. Videos show many frames per second.
a named chunk of stored bytes, such as a document, a photo, or a program.
the rulebook for what a file's bytes mean (.jpg, .mp3, .pdf, .csv). The file extension hints at the format.
"comma-separated values", a plain-text table where each line is a row and commas separate the columns. Spreadsheets can open it.
a plain-text format for structured data using labels and values, like {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}. APIs and AI tools use it constantly.
making data smaller. Lossless compression can be undone perfectly; lossy compression throws away some detail to save more space.
data about data, such as a photo's date, location, and camera model.
an organized collection of examples (texts, images, labeled records) used to train or test AI.
organized storage software designed to save, search, and update large amounts of data quickly.
a microscopic switch controlled by electricity, the basic building block of all chips. Modern chips contain billions.
a material (mainly silicon) whose ability to carry electricity can be controlled. It is what makes transistors possible, and "semiconductor" is also the name of the chip industry.
a small slice of silicon with billions of transistors and wires etched onto it.
a tiny circuit of a few transistors that combines on/off signals by a rule (AND, OR, NOT). Gates combine to do arithmetic.
Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly (later about every two years). It is a trend, not a law of nature, and it has slowed.
the general-purpose processor that runs programs step by step. Very flexible, but does only a few things at once.
one independent processing unit inside a CPU or GPU. More cores means more work done at the same time.
how many basic steps a processor takes per second, measured in gigahertz (billions per second).
a processor with thousands of small cores that do the same math on lots of data at once. Built for graphics, it is now the main engine of AI.
chips designed specially for AI math. Google's Tensor Processing Unit is the best-known non-GPU example.
fast, temporary working space for data the processor is using right now. It is erased when the power goes off.
very fast memory stacked right next to an AI chip so it can be fed numbers quickly. It is often the limiting factor for AI.
slower but permanent places to keep files. Data survives power-off.
a small, very fast memory that keeps recently used data close at hand so it doesn't have to be fetched again.
the ladder from tiny, super-fast memory (registers, cache) to big, slow storage. Good programs keep the data they need near the top.
how much data can be moved per second, like the width of a pipe.
how long one trip takes, from request to the start of a response.
one floating-point operation, a single multiplication or addition of decimal numbers. Used to count how much math a job takes.
floating-point operations per second, a measure of computing speed. Teraflops are trillions and exaflops are quintillions per second.
a computer that provides a service to other computers over a network. It usually has no screen and sits in a rack in a data center.
a building packed with servers, networking gear, power equipment, and cooling. Your chatbot runs in one.
a very large group of processors connected to work on one big problem together. The biggest AI training clusters are effectively supercomputers.
a set of instructions a computer follows. "Software" is the general term for programs, as opposed to physical hardware.
one basic command a processor understands, such as "add these two numbers" or "move this data".
a step-by-step method for solving a problem, like a recipe. It can be written in any programming language, or in plain words.
instructions written in a programming language that humans can read and edit.
a precise artificial language for writing instructions, such as Python, JavaScript, or C++.
a popular, readable programming language that dominates AI work, largely because of its huge collection of ready-made libraries.
the raw binary instructions a processor actually executes.
tools that translate human-written code into something the machine runs. A compiler translates everything first; an interpreter translates and runs line by line.
a named box in a program that holds a value, like price = 20.
the kind of value something is: whole number (integer), decimal (float), text (string), true/false (boolean), list, and so on.
an instruction to repeat steps, such as "for each photo, do this".
a named, reusable block of code that takes inputs and returns an output.
ready-made code others have written that you can reuse. NumPy and PyTorch are libraries.
a bug is a mistake in code that causes wrong behavior. Debugging is finding and fixing it.
a document mixing text and runnable code cells. Colab runs it free in your browser on Google's computers.
the master program (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS) that manages hardware and lets apps run and share resources.
a free, open-source operating system that runs almost all servers, supercomputers, and Android phones.
a program made for users to accomplish tasks, like a chatbot app or a web browser.
the front end is what you see and touch (the app's screen). The back end is the behind-the-scenes servers doing the work.
software whose source code is published so anyone can use, study, change, and share it under a license.
legal terms saying what you may do with code or a model. MIT and Apache 2.0 are permissive; GPL requires sharing changes.
an AI model whose trained numbers (weights) can be downloaded and run by anyone. The training data and code may stay private.
Git tracks every change to code over time. GitHub is a website for storing and collaborating on Git projects.
computers connected so they can exchange data.
the worldwide network of networks, linked by shared rules (protocols).
an agreed set of rules for how computers talk, like etiquette for machines. TCP/IP and HTTP are protocols.
a small chunk of data sent across a network. Big messages are split into many packets and reassembled.
a numeric address identifying a device on the internet, like a postal address.
the internet's phone book, turning names like gemini.google.com into IP addresses.
a web address, specifying the protocol, the site, and the page.
the protocol browsers and apps use to request and receive web content. HTTPS is the encrypted version.
scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it.
the client asks (your phone); the server answers (a computer in a data center).
renting computing power and storage over the internet instead of owning the machines.
a giant cloud provider operating huge data centers worldwide, such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud.
a defined way for one program to request services from another, like a menu and a waiter. AI companies sell model access through APIs.
a secret password-like code identifying who is using an API, so they can be billed and limited.
a cap on how many requests you may make in a period of time.
a traffic director that spreads incoming requests across many servers.
sending a response piece by piece as it is produced, which is why chatbot answers appear word by word.
see entries 42 and 43. How much data, versus how long the trip takes.
a rule that turns each input into an output, like f(x) = 2x + 1. An AI model is a huge function.
a symbol (x, y) standing for a number that can change.
an adjustable number inside a function or model that shapes its behavior. Modern AI models have billions to trillions of them.
the most common kind of parameter. It is a number saying how strongly one input influences an output.
a parameter added after multiplying, which shifts the output up or down. Unrelated to unfair bias.
a straight-line relationship, where doubling the input doubles the effect. Built from multiplying and adding only.
a bend or squash (like "replace negatives with zero") applied between layers. Without it, stacking layers would add no power.
a number giving a position along one direction; (3, 5) is a point on a grid.
an ordered list of numbers, such as [3, 5, 2]. It can describe a point, an arrow, or a thing's features.
how many numbers a vector has, meaning how many directions its space has. AI uses vectors with thousands of dimensions.
a vector that represents a word, image, or item so that similar things get similar vectors.
multiply two vectors entry by entry and add up the results. A big result means they "point the same way".
a similarity score from −1 to 1 based on the angle between two vectors, ignoring their lengths.
a rectangular table of numbers with rows and columns. Neural network layers are matrices.
a matrix or tensor's size, like 3×4 (3 rows, 4 columns). Shapes must match to multiply.
combining two matrices where each output entry is the dot product of a row and a column. It is the most common operation in AI.
a grid of numbers with any number of dimensions: a vector is 1-D, a matrix 2-D, a stack of images 4-D.
growth by repeated multiplying (doubling, tripling), which starts slow and then explodes.
the reverse of an exponential. It answers "what power do I need?", so the log base 10 of 1,000 is 3.
a chart axis where each step multiplies (1, 10, 100, 1,000) instead of adding. It is used to show huge ranges.
a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) measuring how likely something is.
a list of every possible outcome with its probability, all adding up to 1.
a quantity whose value depends on chance, like a die roll.
picking an outcome at random according to a distribution. Chatbots sample each next token.
a setting that makes sampling more predictable (low) or more varied and creative (high).
a formula that turns any list of scores into probabilities that are positive and add to 1.
the probability of something given that something else is true, written P(A | B).
a recipe for updating a belief when new evidence arrives, combining how likely the evidence is with how common the thing was to begin with (the base rate).
how common something is before you look at any specific evidence.
two events are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
the long-run average result if you repeated a random process many times.
the average, the middle value, and the most common value. Three ways to describe a "typical" number.
how spread out numbers are around the average. Standard deviation is the square root of variance, in the original units.
the common hump-shaped pattern where most values sit near the average and extremes are rare.
two things tending to move together. It does not prove that one causes the other.
a value far from the rest that can distort averages.
random variation in data that hides the true pattern.
when a model memorizes its training examples, including their noise, and does badly on new ones. Like memorizing an answer key.
performing well on new, unseen examples. This is the real goal of learning.
the data used to learn, the data used to tune choices, and the data held back for a final honest exam.
how fast one quantity changes as another changes, like miles per hour.
steepness of a line, "rise over run". It is positive going up and negative going down.
the slope of a curve at one exact point. It answers "if I nudge the input a tiny bit, how much does the output change?"
the slope with respect to one knob while holding all the others still.
the list of all partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest increase, so going the opposite way reduces error fastest.
the rule for finding how a change ripples through several connected steps, by multiplying the step-by-step effects.
the efficient method for computing every parameter's gradient in a neural network, working backward from the error using the chain rule.
a formula giving one number for how wrong the model's outputs are. Training tries to make it small.
the standard loss for language models. Roughly, it measures how surprised the model was by the correct next token.
finding the parameter values that make something as good (or as small) as possible.
optimization by repeatedly taking small steps downhill against the gradient.
how big each gradient-descent step is.
gradient descent using a small random handful (batch) of examples per step, which is faster and works well.
a dip that is lower than its surroundings but not the lowest point overall.
the way computers store decimal numbers with a limited number of significant digits, like scientific notation in binary.
how many bits each number uses (32, 16, 8, or 4). Fewer bits are faster and use less memory but are less exact.
storing a model's numbers with fewer bits to make it smaller and faster, with a small loss of accuracy.
the field of making machines do tasks that require intelligence when humans do them.
making computers learn patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules.
a model made of layers of simple units, each computing a weighted sum plus a squash. It is loosely inspired by brain neurons, but it is really stacked matrix math.
machine learning using neural networks with many layers.
the trained function, meaning the architecture plus all its learned parameters.
the process of adjusting a model's parameters using data until it performs well.
using an already-trained model to produce outputs. Every chatbot reply is inference.
a chunk of text (often part of a word) that a language model reads and writes. In English, about four characters or three-quarters of a word on average.
the program that splits text into tokens and converts them to numbers (and back).
the maximum amount of text (in tokens) a model can consider at once, including the conversation so far.
a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. It is the engine inside chatbots.
the neural network design introduced in 2017 that underlies nearly all modern chatbots. Its key ingredient is "attention".
a mechanism letting each token look at all the other tokens and decide, using dot products, which ones matter most.
"Generative Pre-trained Transformer", OpenAI's model family name. It became a generic term.
a model trained to produce a long internal "thinking" process before its final answer, introduced publicly with OpenAI's o1 (September 2024).
an AI system that takes actions toward a goal over multiple steps (searching, clicking, running code), not just answering once.
when a model confidently states something false or made up.
the early approach of programming intelligence as explicit symbols and logical rules ("Good Old-Fashioned AI").
a 1970s–80s program encoding a human expert's knowledge as if-then rules.
the 1950s single-layer learning machine, a single artificial neuron that learns weights from examples.
a period when disappointment caused funding and interest in AI to collapse (roughly the mid-1970s and the late 1980s to early 1990s).
Alan Turing's 1950 proposal to judge machine intelligence by whether a human judge can tell it apart from a person in text conversation.
a standard test used to compare AI systems' performance.
the observed pattern that models predictably improve as you increase compute, data, and parameters together.
shorthand for the amount of computing power (or total operations) used, as in "training compute".
NVIDIA's software platform (2007) that lets programmers use GPUs for general math. It is a major reason NVIDIA dominates AI.

a term coined by Andrej Karpathy in February 2025 for building software by describing what you want to an AI and accepting its code, often without reading it closely. Collins Dictionary's 2025 Word of the Year.
an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 that lets AI apps connect to outside tools and data in a uniform way, like a USB port for AI.
A program whose behavior is entirely spelled out by human-written if-then rules. Also called an "expert system" in older AI.
A parameter that shifts the output up or down regardless of input (the intercept of a line). It is unrelated to unfairness.
A setting chosen by a human before training, such as learning rate, tree depth, or number of clusters. It controls how learning happens but is not itself learned.
One measurable input property of an example, such as square footage, word count, or pixel brightness. A column in a data table.
The correct answer the model should learn to predict for an example, such as "spam" or "$410,000."
One record in a dataset: one email, one house, one image.
The model's output for an input. It can be a number, a category, a probability, or generated text.
A regularity in data, such as "emails with many exclamation marks are often spam," that a model can exploit.
Learning from examples that come with correct answers (labels).
Finding structure, such as groups or simpler representations, in data that has no labels.
Learning from a small labeled set plus a large unlabeled set.
Learning where the labels are created automatically from the data itself, for example by hiding the next word and asking the model to predict it. This is how LLMs are pretrained.
Learning by trial and error: an agent takes actions, receives rewards or penalties, and improves its strategy.
The learner/decision-maker in reinforcement learning.
The world, game or simulation an RL agent acts in.
The numeric score an RL agent receives that tells it how good an outcome was.
An RL agent's strategy: the rule for choosing actions in each situation.
Fine-tuning a model using human judgments (often rankings of two responses) as the reward signal. It is key to how chatbots are made helpful.
Reusing knowledge from a model trained on one task to help with a different task.
Further training an already-trained model on a smaller, specific dataset.
The large first stage of training on broad data, before task-specific fine-tuning.
Doing a task from just a few examples, or none, usually by leveraging a large pretrained model.
A strategy where the model picks which unlabeled examples it would most benefit from having humans label.
Updating a model continuously as new data arrives, rather than training once.
Predicting a number (price, temperature, demand).
Predicting a category (spam/not spam; cat/dog/bird).
Classification with exactly two categories.
Classification with three or more mutually exclusive categories.
Each example can have several labels at once (a photo tagged "beach" and "dog").
Grouping similar examples together without predefined labels.
Compressing many features into fewer while keeping the important information.
Identifying examples that are unusually different from the rest.
A system that predicts what items (movies, products, posts) a person will like.
Data recorded over time in order (daily sales, hourly temperature).
Predicting future values of a time series.
Ordering items by predicted relevance, as search engines and feeds do.
A formula that turns the model's mistakes into a single number. Training tries to make it as small as possible.
The average of squared differences between predictions and true numbers. It punishes big misses heavily.
The average size of the misses, ignoring direction.
The standard loss for classification. It heavily penalizes being confidently wrong.
Gradient descent using small random subsets of data (batches) each step, which is faster and noisier.
The group of examples used for one update step.
One full pass through the entire training dataset.
One parameter update.
When training settles and the loss stops improving meaningfully.
The dividing line (or surface) where a classifier switches from predicting one class to another.
A model's estimated chance (0–1) that an example belongs to a class.
The cutoff that turns a probability into a yes/no decision (often 0.5, but adjustable).
Whether a model's stated confidence matches reality (things it calls "70% likely" happen about 70% of the time).
The data the model learns from.
Held-out data used to compare models and tune hyperparameters during development.
Data locked away until the very end to give an honest final score.
Any data deliberately kept out of training for evaluation.
When a model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it does poorly even on training data.
Systematic error from overly simple assumptions: consistently missing in the same direction.
How much a model's predictions would change if trained on a different sample. High variance means jumpy and overfit.
Making a model more flexible lowers bias but raises variance; good models balance the two.
Any technique that discourages unnecessary complexity to reduce overfitting.
Adding a penalty for large weights. L1 can push some weights to exactly zero (feature selection); L2 shrinks them all.
Halting training when validation performance stops improving.
Splitting data into k parts, training k times with a different part held out each time, and averaging the scores.
Splitting data so each part keeps the same mix of classes as the whole.
When information that wouldn't be available at prediction time sneaks into training, producing falsely good scores.
A simple reference model (such as "always predict the average") that any real model must beat.
Systematically trying hyperparameter settings (grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization) to find the best one on validation data.
"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."
A 2×2 (or larger) table counting correct and incorrect predictions by type.
The model said "yes" and the answer was yes.
The model said "yes" but the answer was no (a false alarm; a "Type I error").
The model said "no" but the answer was yes (a miss; a "Type II error").
The model said "no" and the answer was no.
The share of all predictions that were correct. It is misleading when one class is rare.
Of everything the model flagged as positive, the share that truly was. "When it cries wolf, how often is there a wolf?"
Of all real positives, the share the model caught. "How many wolves did it spot?"
Of all real negatives, the share correctly left alone.
A single number combining precision and recall (their harmonic mean). It is high only when both are high.
A graph of true-positive rate vs. false-positive rate as the threshold slides from strict to lenient.
A single 0.5–1.0 score summarizing the ROC curve: the chance the model ranks a random positive above a random negative.
A graph of precision vs. recall across thresholds. It is more informative than ROC when positives are rare.
When one category vastly outnumbers another (fraud vs. normal transactions).
The square root of MSE, which puts error back into the original units (dollars, degrees).
The share of the variation in the target that the model explains (1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the average).
Mean absolute percentage error: the average miss as a percentage of the true value.
Fits a straight line (or flat plane) through data to predict a number.
Despite the name, a classification method. It squashes a weighted sum into a 0–1 probability with an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve.
The S-shaped curve that maps any number to a value between 0 and 1.
Predicts by looking at the k most similar known examples and taking a vote or average.
A way to measure how alike two examples are (for example, straight-line Euclidean distance or cosine similarity).
A probabilistic classifier that combines evidence from each feature, assuming (naively) that features are independent.
A flowchart of yes/no questions learned from data, ending in predictions at the leaves.
In a tree: a question point / a final answer / how many questions deep the tree goes.
Combining many models so their errors partly cancel out.
Training many models on random resamples of the data and averaging their votes.
A bagged ensemble of decision trees, each also seeing a random subset of features.
Building models in sequence, each focusing on the errors of the ones before.
Boosting where each new tree is fit to the remaining errors using gradient descent ideas.
Popular, fast open-source gradient-boosting libraries that dominate tabular-data competitions.
A classifier that finds the boundary with the widest margin between classes.
A mathematical shortcut that lets linear methods like SVMs draw curved boundaries.
A clustering algorithm that repeatedly assigns points to the nearest of k centers and moves each center to its group's average.
The center point (average) of a cluster.
Building a tree of nested clusters by repeatedly merging the closest groups.
A density-based clustering method that finds arbitrarily shaped clusters and labels sparse points as noise.
Finds a few new combined axes that capture most of the variation in many features.
Techniques for squashing high-dimensional data into a 2-D map that keeps similar items near each other, mainly for visualization.
An anomaly detector based on the idea that odd points can be isolated with fewer random splits.
How many standard deviations a value is from the average. It is a simple anomaly flag.
Recommending items based on the preferences of similar users or similar items.
Recommending items similar in their attributes to ones the user liked.
Breaking a big user × item ratings table into hidden "taste" factors to fill in missing ratings.
Difficulty recommending for new users or new items with no history.
In time series: a long-run upward or downward drift / a repeating cycle (weekly, yearly).
A past value used as an input, for example "sales 7 days ago."
A classic statistical forecasting model built from past values and past errors.
Forecasting with a weighted average that favors recent observations.
Testing a forecasting method by repeatedly training on the past and predicting the next period.
A model pretrained (often on synthetic tables) to make predictions on new spreadsheet-style datasets with little or no training. TabPFN is the best-known example.
How easily a human can understand why a model made a prediction.
A measure of how much each feature contributed to a model's predictions.
Recorded facts or measurements: numbers, text, images, sounds, clicks.
Data organized in rows and columns with a fixed format (spreadsheets, database tables).
Data without a predefined table format: free text, images, audio, video.
Data with some organization but no rigid table, such as JSON or log files.
A feature with a fixed set of categories (color, country).
A feature that is a measured quantity (age, price).
A compressed, column-based file format used for large analytical datasets.
A large collection of text used for training or study.
Automatically downloading and extracting content from websites. A crawler follows links from page to page.
A file on a website telling automated crawlers which parts they may visit. It is a request, not an enforcement mechanism.
An "application programming interface": a structured way for programs to request data or services from another system.
Humans (or models) adding labels to raw data: tagging images, transcribing audio, rating answers.
Image labels: a rectangle around an object / a pixel-precise outline of it.
Human judgments comparing two or more model outputs ("A is better than B"), used to train chatbots.
The trusted correct labels against which predictions or annotators are checked.
How often different human labelers give the same label. Low agreement signals an ambiguous task.
Splitting labeling work into small tasks done by many online workers (for example, Amazon Mechanical Turk).
Fixing or removing incorrect, duplicate, missing or inconsistent data.
An empty cell / filling it with a reasonable estimate (such as the column's median).
Removing repeated or near-identical examples, which is critical for web-scale text.
Creating more useful input features from raw data using domain knowledge.
Turning a category into several yes/no columns (red → [1,0,0]).
Rescaling numeric features to comparable ranges so no feature dominates just by its units.
Classic ways to turn text into numbers by counting words, weighting rare informative words more.
A database storing data in linked tables, queried with SQL.
"Structured Query Language", the standard language for asking questions of relational databases.
A column that uniquely identifies each row / combining two tables on a shared key.
Databases that don't use the classic table model (document, key-value, graph stores).
A database optimized to find items whose embeddings are most similar to a query. It is used in AI search and RAG.
An automated series of steps that moves and transforms data from sources to where it's used.
Extract–Transform–Load (clean before storing) vs. Extract–Load–Transform (store raw, clean later).
A central store of cleaned, structured data organized for analysis and reports.
A large, cheap store of raw data in many formats, cleaned only when needed.
An architecture combining a lake's cheap flexible storage with a warehouse's structure and querying.
How fit data is for its purpose: accurate, complete, consistent, timely, valid, unique.
The record of where data came from and every transformation it went through.
Standard documentation describing a dataset's (or model's) origin, contents, intended uses and limitations.
When incoming data (or the relationship between inputs and answers) changes over time, so a once-good model degrades.
When the collected data doesn't represent the population the model will serve.
When data faithfully records a past that was unfair, so a model learns to repeat it.
A feature that indirectly stands in for a sensitive attribute (zip code standing in for race).
When a model's predictions shape the future data it is trained on (predictive policing sends more patrols, which record more incidents).
The study of whether models treat groups equitably. It includes several competing mathematical definitions.
Data that can identify a person (name, email, ID numbers, face).
Removing identifying details / figuring out who someone is anyway by linking data.
A mathematical guarantee, achieved by adding calibrated noise, that results barely change whether or not any one person's data is included.
Training a shared model across many devices or institutions without centralizing their raw data.
When a model can reproduce exact pieces of its training data, a privacy and copyright concern.
The EU's and California's main personal-data protection laws.
Artificially generated data (by simulation or by AI models) used in place of, or alongside, real data.
Training a smaller "student" model on outputs produced by a larger "teacher" model.
Degradation that can occur when models are trained repeatedly on model-generated data, losing rare patterns and diversity.
Creating extra training examples by modifying existing ones (flipping, cropping or rotating images; paraphrasing text).
Legal rights an author has over original creative works, including control over copying.
A US legal doctrine allowing some unlicensed uses of copyrighted works, judged case by case on four factors.
Laws (EU, UK, Japan, others) allowing automated analysis of content under certain conditions, sometimes with opt-outs.
Paying, or otherwise getting permission, to use data, often through a contract with a publisher or platform.
The idea that AI progress could stall because the supply of high-quality human-generated training data is running out.
A simulated task (a software sandbox, a website clone, a math checker) where a model can practice and get automatically scored. It is increasingly treated as "the new training data."
Looking at data through summaries and charts before modeling, to understand it and spot problems.
An interactive document mixing runnable code, results, charts and notes.
A Python library for working with tables of data ("DataFrames").
The standard Python library for classical machine learning.
A Google-owned website hosting data science competitions, free datasets and notebooks.
A platform hosting millions of shared AI models and hundreds of thousands of datasets.
Tools that automatically try many algorithms and settings to find a good model.
The practices and tools for deploying, monitoring and maintaining ML models in production.
The basic unit. It multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the result through an activation function.
An extra adjustable number added to the weighted sum. It shifts the neuron's threshold up or down. (Not the same as social bias.)
The non-linear "squish" applied after the weighted sum. Without it, any stack of layers would behave like a single straight-line function.
Linear means "output changes proportionally with input" (a straight line). Non-linear means curves, thresholds and bends, which neural networks need to model the real world.
An activation that outputs 0 below a threshold and 1 above it. It was used in early perceptrons but can't be trained with gradients.
An S-shaped activation that squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. Useful for probabilities, but it causes vanishing gradients in deep networks.
Like sigmoid but ranges from −1 to 1, centered on zero.
Outputs the input if positive, otherwise 0. Simple and fast, and it made deep networks much easier to train.
A ReLU variant that lets a small negative slope through, so neurons don't "die" permanently at zero.
A smooth, curved version of ReLU used in GPT-2, BERT and many Transformers.
Another smooth ReLU-like activation (input × sigmoid(input)), common in modern models.
A "gated" feed-forward design where one branch, passed through Swish, multiplies another branch element by element. It is the standard MLP in most current LLMs.
A raw score before softmax. Higher logit means the model favors that option more.
A group of neurons that process inputs in parallel. Networks stack layers so each builds on the previous one.

term: Input layer / hidden layer / output layer
definition: Where data enters, the internal processing stages, and where answers come out.
A layer where every input connects to every neuron. Mathematically, a matrix multiplication plus bias.
Depth is the number of layers; width is the number of neurons per layer.
The core arithmetic operation of neural networks: many multiply-and-add operations done at once. GPUs are built to do it fast.
Running inputs through the network, layer by layer, to get an output.

term: Dataset / training set / validation set / test set
definition: The examples used to learn, to tune choices during development, and to give a final honest score on unseen data.
The correct answer attached to a training example (e.g., "cat").
A single number measuring how wrong the model is. Training tries to make it small.
Loss for predicting categories or next tokens. It measures how surprised the model is by the correct answer.
A language-model score derived from cross-entropy: roughly "how many equally likely choices the model feels it's picking between." Lower is better.
Software that records the forward computation and computes gradients automatically, so programmers never derive them by hand.
A plan for changing the learning rate over training, e.g. warm up from tiny, then decay.
Starting training with a very small learning rate and ramping up, to avoid early instability.
Common schedules. Cosine decay smoothly lowers the rate along a cosine curve. WSD holds it flat, then drops it quickly near the end.
A group of examples processed together in one step, and how many are in it.
One parameter update.
The algorithm that turns gradients into parameter updates (SGD, Adam, AdamW, Muon...).
An optimizer trick that keeps a running average of past gradients, like a ball rolling downhill that keeps its speed through small bumps.
An optimizer (2014) that combines momentum with per-parameter adaptive step sizes. The default for most deep learning for a decade.
Adam with weight decay applied separately ("decoupled"), the standard for training Transformers.

An optimizer (Keller Jordan, Dec 2024) that takes the momentum update for each weight matrix and "orthogonalizes" it (via Newton–Schulz iterations) so no single direction dominates. Used at trillion-parameter scale by Kimi K2 and DeepSeek V4.
Other optimizers. Lion uses only the sign of the update. Shampoo and SOAP use richer curvature information ("second-order-ish").
Gently shrinking weights toward zero every step, discouraging overly complex solutions.
How weights are set before training. They must be random (to break symmetry) and correctly scaled (Xavier/Glorot, He initialization).
Randomly switching off a fraction of neurons during training so the network can't rely on any single one. Turned off at inference.
A layer that rescales activations to a standard range so training stays stable.
Normalizes each feature using statistics from the current batch. Key for CNNs.
Normalizes across the features of each single example. Standard in Transformers.
A simpler, cheaper layer norm that only rescales by the root-mean-square (no mean subtraction). Used in Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, etc.
Whether normalization is applied before or after each sub-layer. Pre-norm trains more stably in deep Transformers.
Error signals shrink as they travel back through many layers, so early layers stop learning.
Error signals grow uncontrollably, making training blow up.
Capping the size of gradients to prevent explosions.
Adding a layer's input back to its output (output = input + layer(input)), giving signals and gradients a highway around each layer. This made 100+-layer networks trainable.
In a Transformer, the running vector each token carries through all layers, which every layer reads and adds to.
2024–25 generalizations of residual connections with several parallel streams that mix. DeepSeek's mHC constrains the mixing to keep training stable.
A sudden jump in training loss, often a sign of instability. Expensive at frontier scale.
Storing and computing numbers with fewer bits to go faster and use less memory, while keeping key quantities in higher precision.
A result (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991) that a network with one wide enough hidden layer can approximate any reasonable function. It guarantees existence, not that training will find it.
Assumptions baked into a model's design that make some solutions easier to learn, e.g. CNNs assume nearby pixels matter together.
Rich Sutton's 2019 essay arguing that, over decades, general methods that scale with computation beat approaches built on human-crafted knowledge.
A pattern a network has learned to detect internally, such as an edge, a texture, or the concept "legal language".
The phenomenon of networks packing more features than they have neurons by overlapping them, which makes interpretability hard.
The surprising observation that test error can fall, rise, then fall again as models grow past the point of fitting training data exactly.
A network of stacked dense layers. Also the name for the feed-forward block in Transformers.
A network that slides small learned filters across images (or audio) to detect local patterns, reusing the same weights everywhere.
Sliding a small grid of weights over the input and computing a weighted sum at each position.
The small grid of learned weights used in a convolution, e.g. 3×3.
The output grid of a convolution, showing where the filter's pattern was found.
How far the filter jumps each move, and the border added so the filter can cover edges.
One "layer" of an image or feature map (red, green and blue are 3 channels; deep layers may have hundreds).
Shrinking a feature map by keeping the max or average of each small region, making detection robust to small shifts.
The region of the original input that a given neuron can "see". It grows with depth.
A 2015 CNN family that introduced residual connections and trained 152-layer networks.
An encoder–decoder CNN with skip connections between matching resolutions. The classic denoiser in diffusion models.
A network that processes sequences one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward as memory.
The internal memory vector an RNN (or SSM) carries from step to step.
An RNN (1997) with gates that decide what to forget, store and output, so it can remember over longer spans.
A simpler gated RNN with two gates instead of three.
A learned 0-to-1 multiplier that controls how much information flows, like a valve.
An encoder reads an input sequence and a decoder writes an output sequence (e.g., translation).
The part that turns input into an internal representation / the part that turns a representation into output.
The "map" where embeddings live. Directions and distances carry meaning.
A 2013 method that learns word embeddings by predicting nearby words. It famously supports analogies like king − man + woman ≈ queen.
The program that splits text into tokens. Byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging frequent character pairs.
The fixed list of all tokens a model knows (often 100k–250k).
Information added so the model knows the order of tokens.
Encodes position by rotating query and key vectors by position-dependent angles, so attention naturally depends on relative distance.
Attention where a sequence attends to itself (each token looks at the other tokens of the same text).
Attention where one sequence looks at another (e.g., image denoiser attending to text-prompt embeddings).
Three vectors each token produces: what it's looking for, what it offers as a label, and the content it hands over if selected.
The softmaxed scores saying how much each token attends to each other token.
Running several attention operations in parallel with different learned projections, each capturing different relationships.
Ways to shrink attention memory. Several query heads share keys/values (multi-query, grouped-query), or keys/values are compressed into a small latent (multi-head latent attention).
Blocks each token from attending to future tokens, so the model learns to predict the next token honestly.
Transformer layouts. BERT-style (understanding), GPT-style (generating; all major chatbots), T5/Whisper-style (input→output transformation).
The per-token MLP inside each Transformer block.
Stored keys and values from earlier tokens so generation doesn't recompute them. It grows with conversation length.
Generating one piece at a time, each conditioned on everything generated so far.
Sampling settings. Temperature flattens or sharpens the probability distribution. Top-p samples only from the smallest set of tokens covering p% probability.
A GPU-efficient way to compute exact attention in tiles without storing the full attention matrix.
Each token attends only to the last N tokens, which caps cost.
Each token attends to a selected subset of earlier tokens (e.g., DeepSeek Sparse Attention picks the top-k relevant ones).
The tendency of models to dump excess attention on the first token. Some designs add an explicit learnable sink, others remove the need via gating.
A Transformer that splits an image into patches and treats each patch as a token.
A small square of an image (or a small spacetime block of video) used as one token.
A layer containing many expert sub-networks plus a router that activates only a few per token, giving huge total capacity at modest compute.
The small network in an MoE that scores experts and picks which ones process each token.
All parameters stored vs. those actually used for one token (e.g., 1.6T total, 49B active).
A network that operates on nodes and edges, updating each node from its neighbors ("message passing").
A sequence model that keeps a fixed-size internal state updated each step (like an RNN) but is designed for fast parallel training.
A 2023 selective state-space model whose state update depends on the input, letting it choose what to remember. Successors are Mamba-2 (2024) and Mamba-3 (2026).

term: Linear attention / DeltaNet / Gated DeltaNet / KDA
definition: Attention variants that replace the growing token-by-token comparison with a fixed-size memory updated per token. Gates and the "delta rule" control what is overwritten.
A model mixing layer types, typically mostly linear/SSM layers plus some full-attention layers.
Training embeddings by pulling matching pairs together and pushing non-matching pairs apart.
OpenAI's 2021 model that learned a shared space for images and text from about 400 million image–caption pairs.
Performing a task without any task-specific training examples.
A model that handles more than one data type (text, images, audio, video).
Combining modalities from the very first layer vs. bolting a separate encoder onto a language model.
A model that learns the distribution of data so it can produce new samples (text, images, sound).
The compressed internal space of representations. Moving through it smoothly changes the generated output.
A network trained to compress input to a small code and reconstruct it.
An autoencoder whose code is a probability region, making its latent space smooth and sample-able.
A generator and a discriminator trained against each other until the fakes are convincing.
A GAN failure where the generator produces only a few kinds of outputs.
A generator trained to reverse a gradual noising process. It creates data by denoising random static step by step.
Removing predicted noise / the plan for how much noise is present at each step.
The algorithm and number of steps used to go from noise to image. Fewer steps is faster but sometimes worse.
Making outputs follow the prompt more strongly by contrasting the model's prediction with and without the prompt (the "guidance scale").
Text describing what you *don't* want, used in place of the empty prompt during guidance.
The number that fixes the starting random noise, so the same seed and settings reproduce the same image.
Running diffusion in a VAE's compressed latent space instead of on full-resolution pixels, the key efficiency trick behind Stable Diffusion.
A diffusion model whose denoiser is a Transformer over latent patches rather than a U-Net. Standard for modern image and video generators.
A training method where the model learns a velocity field that moves noise to data along straight-ish paths, enabling efficient, few-step generation.
Training a faster "student" model to mimic a slower "teacher", e.g. generating an image in 1–4 steps instead of 50.
An add-on that steers a diffusion model with structure such as poses, edges or depth maps.
A cheap fine-tuning method that trains small add-on matrices instead of all weights. Widely used for custom image styles.
Regenerating a masked region inside an image / extending an image beyond its borders.
A text generator that refines many masked tokens in parallel over several steps instead of writing strictly left to right.
A model that predicts how an environment evolves, especially in response to actions, sometimes rendering it interactively.
Yann LeCun's approach of predicting missing parts in embedding space rather than pixel by pixel.
The most widely used deep-learning library (Meta-originated, now under the PyTorch Foundation). Python-first and flexible.
Google's deep-learning library (2015). Large production install base, less used in new research.
A high-level, beginner-friendly API for building networks. Keras 3 runs on TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch.
Google's library for fast numerical computing with automatic differentiation and compilation, widely used on TPUs at Google DeepMind.
Chips specialized for parallel arithmetic (graphics processing unit; Google's tensor processing unit).
NVIDIA's GPU programming platform / a Python-like language for writing GPU code / a single optimized GPU routine.
The saved parameters of a model (e.g., .safetensors), which is what "open weights" means.
The numbers flowing through a neural network at a given moment while it processes input. Interpretability studies these to see what the model is "thinking."
In a mixture-of-experts model, the subset of weights actually used for each token. This drives speed and cost per token.
A small add-on set of weights trained to specialize a model without changing the original weights. Cheap enough to do on one GPU.
A mode in which the model decides for itself how much to reason before answering, steered by an "effort" setting. It is the default on current Claude models.
Using an AI agent that reads a codebase, edits files, runs tests, and iterates, rather than just suggesting snippets.
Making an AI system's goals and behavior match what its developers and users intend, including being honest and avoiding harm.
Lowering the learning rate toward the end of training, often while switching to the highest-quality data. It "settles" the model.
Measures that make a model's outputs less useful for copying it, such as hiding raw reasoning or detecting mass-extraction accounts.
A family of puzzle benchmarks by François Chollet's ARC Prize, designed to test learning new skills from few examples. ARC-AGI-3 (2026) uses interactive games with no instructions.
A diagram, produced by interpretability tools, of which internal features caused which others on the way to an output.
The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to an error, so every weight can be adjusted slightly.
A model straight out of pretraining. It continues text but doesn't reliably follow instructions or behave like an assistant.
Processing many examples or users together on the same hardware to use it efficiently.
An API option where you submit many requests to be processed within hours instead of seconds, usually at about half price.
When test questions leak into training data, inflating scores without real ability.
When top models score near the maximum, so the test can no longer tell them apart.
Generating N candidate answers and picking the best one with a scorer or verifier.
16-bit number formats used for model weights and training. They use 2 bytes per number.
A tokenizer-building method that starts from bytes or characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.
Intermediate reasoning text a model writes before its final answer.
The exact format, with special tokens marking roles like system, user, and assistant, used to turn a conversation into one token sequence.
A saved snapshot of a model's weights during or after training.
The 2022 finding that, for a given compute budget, parameters and training tokens should grow together, roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
A set of connected internal features and weights that together implement a specific behavior.
A separate model that flags risky inputs or outputs, used to block requests or route them to a safer model.
A model whose weights are not released and which you can only use via the maker's app or API.
A nonprofit's free, massive archive of web pages. It is the raw material for most pretraining datasets.
Summarizing older parts of a long agent session so it fits in the context window and the agent can keep working.
The allocation of model size versus data that gives the lowest loss for a given training compute.
Anthropic's method (2022) of training with AI feedback guided by a written list of principles, reducing the need for human harm labels.
A public document describing how a lab wants its model to think, prioritize, and behave.
A serving technique that adds and removes requests from a running batch token by token, instead of waiting for all to finish.
Cleaning, filtering, deduplicating, and balancing raw data before training.
The recipe of what share of training tokens come from each source: web, code, math, books, languages, synthetic.
The output-generation phase, producing one token per step. It is limited by memory bandwidth.
Removing benchmark questions from training data.
Premium settings that spend far more compute per answer, often running many reasoning paths in parallel.
A model that uses all of its weights for every token. Contrast with MoE.
A simpler alternative to RLHF that learns directly from "A is better than B" pairs, without a separate reward model.
A user- or developer-set dial (e.g., low/medium/high/xhigh/max) for how much a reasoning model thinks.
Skills that seem to appear suddenly as models scale. Whether they are truly sudden is debated.
One full pass through a dataset. Frontier pretraining sees most data roughly once.
Any systematic test of model behavior: benchmarks, red-teaming, human ratings, or task trials.
One of many sub-networks inside a mixture-of-experts layer. Experts specialize in token patterns, not neat human topics.
Anthropic's earlier name for a manual mode with a fixed thinking-token budget. It has been replaced by adaptive thinking on new models.
A direction in a model's internal activations that corresponds to a concept (e.g., "Golden Gate Bridge," "code bug," "sarcasm").
Including a few worked examples in the prompt so the model copies the pattern.
Floating-point operation(s), a single multiply or add. Training budgets are quoted in total FLOPs (e.g., 1e26 = 100 trillion trillion).
8-bit and 4-bit number formats. Newer chips do math in these to go faster and use less memory.
One of the most capable models in existence at a given time.
The model outputs a structured request (e.g., "search('weather Paris')") that software executes, then the result is fed back.
A file format for quantized open-weight models, used by llama.cpp, Ollama, and LM Studio.
A benchmark of very hard, "Google-proof" graduate-level science multiple-choice questions. It is now near-saturated (Kimi K3 reports 93.5%).
Always picking the single most likely next token.
Tying a model's answer to provided sources (search results, documents) rather than memory.
An RL method (DeepSeek, 2024). It samples several answers per prompt and rewards each by how much better it is than the group average.
Rules, filters, and classifiers around a model that block or modify unsafe inputs and outputs.
The software around a model during a task (prompts, tools, memory handling, retries). It can change benchmark scores dramatically.
A 2,500-question public benchmark of expert-level questions, released January 2025 by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI.
Mixing a few full-attention layers with many cheaper linear or sparse attention layers to handle long contexts efficiently.
Training a model to rank instructions by source (system > developer > user > tool output) so injected text can't override the operator.
Fine-tuning on many (instruction, good response) examples so the model follows requests.
Integer formats using 8 or 4 bits per weight. Used to shrink models for cheaper or local inference.
Reverse-engineering a model's internal computations into understandable parts.
A prompt crafted to make a model ignore its safety training.
A term in RL training that keeps the updated model from drifting too far from its starting point (the "leash").
The date after which the model has little or no training data.
A neural network, usually a Transformer, trained on huge text corpora to predict tokens. Now often multimodal.
Using one model to grade another's outputs, often against a rubric.
The raw scores a model gives each vocabulary token before they are converted to probabilities.
Contexts of hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens, and the techniques that make them work.
The tendency to use information at the start and end of a long context better than information in the middle.
A number measuring how wrong the model is. Training tries to lower it.
Sampling several reasoning paths and taking the most common final answer.
The fraction of the hardware's theoretical peak math actually achieved during training, often 25–50%.
An intermediate training stage after bulk pretraining, using curated high-quality, long-context, or reasoning-heavy data.
The part of each Transformer block that processes each token individually. Much of the stored knowledge lives here.
A 2020 benchmark of 57 school and professional subjects in multiple-choice format. It is saturated for frontier models.
A document published with a model describing intended use, training, evaluations, safety testing, and limitations.
Combining weights of two or more fine-tuned models into one, without further training.
A feature that corresponds to one clean concept, the goal of sparse autoencoders.
Handling more than one type of data, such as text, images, audio, or video.
Training the model to predict several future tokens at once, for better learning and faster decoding.
A single model that takes in and produces text, audio, and images directly, rather than chaining separate speech and text models.
A long-context test that hides a fact in a huge document and asks the model to find it.
The pretraining task of predicting the next token given all previous tokens.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p (e.g., 0.9).
The student generates its own answers and the teacher grades each token. This combines RL's realism with distillation's dense feedback.
Strictly, open weights plus open training code and data. It is often used loosely to mean open-weight.
A grader that scores only the final answer.
Training a model on far more tokens than compute-optimal, making it smaller and cheaper to run for its ability.
A memory-management method (vLLM) that stores the KV cache in small pages so many requests share GPU memory efficiently.
One learned number in the model. Frontier models have hundreds of billions to trillions.
A consistent character or style a model adopts, shaped by post-training and system prompts.
How the model knows the order of tokens. RoPE encodes position as rotations of vectors.
Everything after pretraining (SFT, preference learning, RL, safety training) that turns a base model into a product.
A classic RL algorithm (2017) that makes cautious, clipped updates. It was the workhorse of early RLHF.
Processing the whole prompt in parallel before the first output token. It is compute-bound.
A lab's published policy defining dangerous-capability thresholds (e.g., OpenAI's High/Critical; Anthropic's ASL levels) and required safeguards.
A grader that scores each intermediate reasoning step, not just the final answer.
The input text, plus any images or files, you give a model.
Reusing the stored KV cache for a repeated prompt prefix. Labs bill cached input at a steep discount.
Malicious instructions hidden in content the model reads (a web page, an email) that try to hijack it.
Training with low precision simulated, so the final low-bit model loses little quality.
Searching documents and inserting relevant passages into the prompt so answers are grounded.
Deliberately attacking a model to find harmful or unsafe behaviors before release.
A model declining a request. Over-refusal means declining harmless ones.
Generating many outputs and keeping only those that pass a check, often to build training data.
When a model finds a loophole that scores well on the reward without doing the intended task (e.g., editing tests so they pass).
A model trained to output a score predicting how good a response is, usually from human preferences.
Reinforcement learning from AI feedback, where an AI judge supplies the preference labels.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human preferences, then optimize the model against it.
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, rewarding outputs that pass an objective check such as a correct answer or passing tests.
The component that picks which expert (in MoE) or which model (in products like GPT-5) handles an input.
A model improving by generating its own challenges or opponents and learning from the outcomes.
Training on examples of desired input-output behavior.
A tool trained to rewrite a model's activations as a combination of a few interpretable features out of many.
A fast draft guesses several tokens ahead and the big model verifies them all at once, speeding generation without changing outputs.
Changing model behavior by directly adding or removing a feature direction in its activations.
A benchmark of real GitHub issues that a model must fix so the repository's tests pass. "Verified" is a human-checked 500-task subset; harder successors include SWE-bench Pro.
Telling users what they want to hear (agreeing, flattering) instead of what's true.
Hidden or developer-provided instructions at the start of the context that set the model's role, rules, and tools.
A benchmark of tasks an agent must complete in a computer terminal (installing, debugging, data work).
Computation spent when answering (thinking longer, sampling more) rather than during training.
Tokens the model generates while reasoning. You usually pay for them even if they're hidden or summarized.
How many tokens a system produces per second across all users.
The length of task, measured in how long it takes a skilled human, that an AI agent completes with 50% (or 80%) reliability.
Sampling only among the k most likely tokens.
One large training job, from initialization to final checkpoint.
An interpretability tool, a cousin of the SAE, that approximates a layer's input-to-output computation with sparse features.
Gated access to more capable or less restricted model versions for vetted organizations (e.g., cybersecurity defenders).
A program or model that checks whether an answer is correct (a unit test, a math checker, a proof assistant).
The component that turns an image into tokens the language model can attend to.
The learned parameter values. "Releasing the weights" means publishing them for download.
The billions of adjustable numbers inside a model that were set during training. More parameters roughly means more capacity, plus more memory and cost.
Having no memory between requests. LLM APIs are stateless, so the app must re-send the conversation every time.
When a model states something false but plausible, such as a fake citation or invented statistic.
A model trained to "think" in hidden steps before answering. It is better at math, code and planning, but slower and costlier.
A setting on many reasoning models that controls how much they think. Low is fast and cheap, high is thorough.
A model you can only use through the maker's app or API.
The turns of a conversation. "User" is what the human (or program) sends. "Assistant" is what the model replied.
The craft of writing prompts that reliably get the output you want.
Deciding everything that goes into the model's context window at each step (instructions, documents, tool results, memory, history), not just the wording of the prompt.
Telling the model who to be ("You are an experienced tax accountant") to focus its tone and expertise.
Giving no examples, one example, or several examples of the desired input→output in the prompt. Few-shot is also called multishot.
A marker that separates parts of a prompt, such as triple quotes, Markdown headings, or XML tags.
Labels in angle brackets like <document>…</document> that wrap sections of a prompt so the model knows what is an instruction and what is data.
A simple text formatting style (# for headings, * for bullets) that models read and write fluently.
Getting a model to reason step by step before giving its final answer, which improves multi-step problems.
Splitting a task into a sequence of prompts where each output feeds the next.
Asking a model to write or improve a prompt.
A reusable prompt with blanks (variables) such as {{customer_email}} that get filled in automatically.
Writing the beginning of the model's answer yourself so it continues from there. Newer Claude models (4.6 and later) no longer accept it on the final turn.
The decline in a model's recall and accuracy as its context window fills with more and more tokens.
Another randomness control that limits choices to the most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to p.
The cap you set on how long the model's response may be. Hitting it cuts the answer off.
The API's note on why generation ended: finished naturally, hit max tokens, wants to call a tool, or refused.
Preferences you set once ("I'm a teacher; be concise") that the app adds to every chat.
Facts the app saves about you, or past chats it can search, inserted into new conversations. You can view, edit or turn it off.
A chat that isn't saved to history or memory.
A workspace grouping chats with shared files and instructions (and, in Claude, a separate memory) so every chat in it starts with the same background.
A personalized assistant (OpenAI's and Google's names) with its own instructions, knowledge files and tools, shareable with others.
A side panel where the AI builds and edits a document, code, or a small interactive app alongside the chat.
A mode where the AI spends minutes running many searches and reading sources, then writes a long report with citations.
Talking to the AI with your voice and hearing it answer in near real time.
An add-on that lets a chat app reach another service (Gmail, Drive, Slack, GitHub), often built on MCP.
A chat-app feature where the AI carries out multi-step tasks (browsing, filling forms, editing files) rather than just answering.
A specific web address on an API that performs one kind of task, e.g. "send messages to a model".
The standard web conversation: your program sends a request (method, address, headers, body) and the server sends back a response (status code, body).
A number summarizing the result: 200 = OK, 400 = bad request, 401 = bad API key, 429 = too many requests, 5xx = server problem.
A way to store a key outside your code so it isn't accidentally shared.
A ready-made library that makes calling an API easier from a given programming language.
A description of what a JSON object must look like (which fields, which types, which are required).
A text window where you type commands to your computer. Many coding agents run there.
Requests per minute and tokens per minute, the usual units of rate limits.
Retrying a failed request after waiting longer each time (1s, 2s, 4s…) to avoid hammering a busy server.
The web technique most LLM APIs use to stream tokens to your program.
How long until the first word appears. It dominates how fast an app *feels*.
How fast the model produces text once it starts.
One million tokens, the standard unit in API price lists ("$2 / MTok").
What you send vs. what the model writes. Output usually costs 4–6× more per token.
Whether a request reused a cached prefix (hit, cheap) or had to process it fresh (miss, full price).
An API feature that forces the model's answer to match a JSON Schema exactly.
The technique behind structured outputs. At each step the model is only allowed to pick tokens that keep the output valid.
Popular Python / TypeScript libraries for defining data shapes and validating them. AI SDKs use them to define schemas.
Using a fixed model version ID so behavior doesn't change under you without warning.
A provider announcing, then executing, the shutdown of an old model version.
An arrangement where the provider doesn't store your prompts and outputs after processing.
Guaranteeing your data is processed in a specific region (e.g., US or EU), often for a price premium.
How many numbers are in an embedding (often 256–3,072). Each is a direction on the "map of meaning".
Finding text by meaning rather than exact words, using embeddings.
Classic search that scores documents by matching words, with BM25 the standard formula. It is great for names, codes and rare terms.
Combining keyword and semantic search results to get the strengths of both.
A simple method to merge ranked lists from different searches into one.
Fast search methods that find "close enough" nearest vectors among millions without checking every one. HNSW is the most common.
Restricting search to items with certain tags (date, author, access rights) before or after the vector search.
Loading and preparing source documents for a RAG system.
Extracting text from files. OCR (optical character recognition) reads text from images and scans.
Splitting documents into smaller passages for embedding and retrieval.
Repeating a little text between adjacent chunks so ideas cut at a boundary aren't lost.
Adding a short, AI-written explanation of where a chunk fits in its document before embedding it, to improve search.
The component of a RAG system that finds candidate passages for a query.
The number of best-matching results returned (e.g., top-5).
A second model that reads the query and each candidate together and re-scores them more accurately than the first search.
Rephrasing or splitting a user question to improve search results.
Having the model draft a fake answer, then searching for real documents similar to that draft.
RAG where the model itself decides when, what and how many times to search.
Data stored as entities (people, companies) connected by labeled relationships ("works for", "acquired").
A RAG approach (popularized by Microsoft Research) that builds a knowledge graph from documents and summarizes clusters of it, helping answer broad "big picture" questions.
A pointer from part of an answer to the source passage that supports it.
Whether an answer is actually supported by the retrieved sources.
Of the passages that *should* have been found, how many appeared in the top k results.
Fine-tuning on example pairs of input → ideal output.
Fine-tuning on pairs of better vs. worse answers so the model learns which you prefer. DPO (direct preference optimization) is a popular method.
Fine-tuning where a grader scores the model's attempts and the model is rewarded for higher scores.
The small trained add-on file from LoRA that changes a base model's behavior. It can be swapped in and out.
LoRA performed on a model compressed to 4-bit precision, so large models can be fine-tuned on one GPU.
The graphics processor that runs AI fast, and its dedicated memory. A model must fit in (V)RAM to run well.
Memory shared by CPU and GPU (e.g., Apple Silicon Macs), which lets laptops run surprisingly large local models.
A free tool for downloading and running open models locally with one command, plus a local API.
A desktop app for finding, downloading and chatting with local models, with a local server mode.
An open-source C/C++ engine that runs LLMs efficiently on ordinary hardware. Many local tools are built on it.
A high-performance open-source server for running models for many users at once.
A model's ability to request that your software run a named function (search, calculator, database query) with specific inputs.
The name, description and input schema that tell the model what a tool does and how to call it.
The model's structured request to use a tool, and the output your software sends back.
A tool the AI provider runs for you (e.g., web search, code execution).
A tool your own code runs when the model asks.
The model requesting several tool calls at once to save time.
A sandboxed tool where the model writes and runs code (often Python) to calculate, analyze files or make charts.
The cycle at the heart of every agent: think → act → observe → repeat until done.
An influential pattern (Reason + Act) where the model alternates written reasoning with tool actions.
An agent breaking a goal into steps or a to-do list and updating it as it learns.
A system where *code* fixes the sequence of LLM steps. In an agent, *the model* chooses the steps.
Classifying a request and sending it to the right prompt, model or specialist.
A pattern where a lead model splits a task and delegates parts to worker models, then combines results.
A loop where one model produces work and another critiques it until it's good enough.
Several agents with different roles or contexts collaborating on a task.
A helper agent spawned by a main agent for a focused subtask, with its own clean context, that reports back a summary.
Transferring a conversation or task from one agent to another, more specialized one.
Design where a person must review or approve certain steps (e.g., before sending money).
Short-term is what's in the current context. Long-term is stored externally (files, databases) and recalled later.
Memory of past events, of facts, and of how to do things (skills), respectively.
An agent that runs on a remote machine for minutes to hours while you do other things, then reports back (e.g., opens a pull request).
An agent run set to happen automatically at set times or on events.
An open standard (launched by Anthropic, Nov 2024, now under the Linux Foundation) that lets AI apps connect to external tools and data through a common "plug".
The host is the AI app. It creates one client per connection, and each client talks to a server, the program that exposes tools and data.
The three things a server can offer: actions to run, data to read, and reusable prompt templates.
How MCP messages travel. stdio connects to a program on your own machine, and Streamable HTTP connects to a remote server over the web.
The simple request/response message format MCP and A2A are built on.
The standard "Log in with…/Allow access" system that lets an app use your account on another service without seeing your password.
An MCP extension letting servers show interactive user interfaces (forms, charts, widgets) inside the chat.
A directory where MCP servers are listed so clients can find and install them.
An open standard (started by Google, now at the Linux Foundation) for agents from different vendors to discover each other and delegate tasks.
A public description file in A2A that advertises what an agent can do and how to reach it.
A folder-based open format for packaging instructions, scripts and resources an agent loads only when relevant.
Loading only a short summary of each skill or tool at first, and the full details only when needed, to save context.
Plain-text instruction files placed in a project that coding agents read automatically (project conventions, commands, do's and don'ts).
A user-defined script that runs automatically at certain points in an agent's work (e.g., format code after every edit, block dangerous commands).
A bundle of skills, tools/MCP servers, hooks and sub-agents installable as one package.
An agent controlling a computer by looking at screenshots and issuing mouse clicks and keystrokes.
An agent that operates a web browser to navigate sites, fill forms and extract information.
An agent specialized in software work: reading code, editing files, running tests and commands, and opening pull requests.
The app programmers write code in (e.g., VS Code, JetBrains, Cursor).
Git tracks every change to code. A repository is a project's folder plus history. A commit is a saved change. A pull request (PR) proposes changes for review before merging.
The disciplined alternative: write a clear spec, have agents implement it in small reviewed steps with tests.
A coding-agent setting where the agent investigates and proposes a plan for approval before changing anything.
An isolated environment (container, virtual machine) where an agent can run code without being able to harm your real system or data.
A code library for building agents (e.g., OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Google ADK).
A larger, opinionated toolkit (e.g., LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI) that structures how you build LLM apps.
Building software by connecting visual blocks instead of (or with very little) writing code.
In automation tools, the event that starts a workflow (new email) and the steps it performs (summarize, post to Slack).
A URL that receives an automatic message when something happens elsewhere. It is how apps "call" automations.
A service (Lovable, Bolt, Replit, v0) that generates and hosts a working web app from a text description.
Systematic tests that measure how well an AI system performs on your tasks.
A curated set of realistic test inputs with known good answers or grading rubrics.
A written scoring guide listing what makes an answer good or bad.
Showing two versions to different users and comparing results statistically.
Recording what happened inside an AI system (every call, tool use, token count, delay) so you can debug and improve it.
One recorded step (span), and the full tree of steps for a request (trace).
The practices and tools for deploying, monitoring, versioning and improving LLM applications in production.
A middle layer that sends requests to different models or providers, handling fallbacks, budgets and logging.
Trying a cheap model first and escalating to an expensive one only if needed.
A model that flags harmful or off-policy content.
Data that identifies a person (names, emails, ID numbers), often required to be detected and redacted.
Direct comes from the user typing it. Indirect is hidden inside content the AI reads, such as a web page, PDF or tool result.
Getting an AI system to leak private data to an attacker, e.g., by embedding it in a link or sending it via a tool.
Simon Willison's term for the dangerous combination of private data access, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally.
Hiding malicious instructions in a tool's description or output so an agent misbehaves.
Giving an AI more permissions or autonomy than its task needs (an OWASP top-10 risk).
Giving each user, tool or agent only the minimum access it needs.
Deliberately attacking your own system to find weaknesses before others do.
Employees using unapproved AI tools at work.
People's tendency to over-trust automated suggestions and stop checking them.
Two product stances. A copilot suggests and the human decides. An autopilot acts on its own within limits.
Interfaces the AI creates on the fly (charts, forms, mini-apps) rather than only text.
Many transistors and wires manufactured together on one piece of silicon. "Chip" and "IC" mean the same thing.
A single rectangular piece of silicon cut from a wafer, containing one chip's circuitry. A product may contain several dies in one package.
How many times per second a chip's internal metronome ticks. 2 GHz means 2 billion ticks per second, and work happens in step with these ticks.
