A single sequence of instructions being executed. One core can juggle one or more threads.
The "vocabulary" of commands a processor understands. Examples are x86 (Intel/AMD), Arm (phones, Apple Macs, NVIDIA Grace/Vera, Google Axion) and RISC-V (an open standard).
A company (and the ISA it licenses) whose energy-efficient CPU designs are used in nearly all phones and increasingly in data-center CPUs.
A free, open instruction set anyone can use without license fees. It is popular with startups and in some AI chips (e.g., Meta's MTIA, Tenstorrent).
The historical rule that smaller transistors used proportionally less power. It broke down in the mid-2000s, which ended rapid clock-speed increases and pushed chips toward parallelism.
The slowdown caused by having to shuttle data back and forth between separate processor and memory. It is the root of today's "memory wall."
Doing many operations at the same time instead of one after another. It is the central idea behind GPUs and AI accelerators.
"Single Instruction, Multiple Data / Threads": one command applied to many numbers at once, like a drill sergeant ordering a whole platoon to step forward.
The core operation of neural networks: combining two grids of numbers by many multiply-and-add steps. GEMM ("general matrix multiply") is the technical name.
One multiplication followed by adding the result to a running total. One MAC counts as 2 FLOPs.
One arithmetic operation (like a multiply or add) on decimal-style numbers. Used as a *count* of total work, e.g., "trained with 10^26 FLOP."
Floating-point operations *per second*. A *speed*, e.g., an H100 delivers ~10^15 FLOP/s (1 petaFLOPS) in BF16.
Prefixes for 10^12, 10^15, 10^18 and 10^21. An exaFLOP is a billion billion operations.
Trillions of operations per second. It is usually quoted for integer math on phone/laptop NPUs and is not directly comparable to FLOPS.
Peak is the theoretical maximum on a spec sheet. Achieved is what real software gets (often 30–60% of peak for training).
"Sparse" figures assume a special 2:4 pattern where half the numbers are zero and can be skipped, which doubles the headline number. Dense figures are the realistic baseline.
How many math operations are performed for each byte of data moved from memory. High intensity keeps compute busy; low intensity leaves it waiting on memory.
A chart showing whether a workload is limited by compute (flat "roof") or by memory bandwidth (sloped "roof"), based on its arithmetic intensity.
Whether a task is slowed mainly by the speed of math or by the speed of fetching data.
Rule of thumb: training a dense transformer takes about 6 × (number of parameters) × (number of training tokens) FLOPs.
The exponent sets how big or small the number is (range). The mantissa sets how many significant digits it keeps (detail).
64-bit "double precision," used in scientific simulation. It is mostly irrelevant for AI and increasingly de-emphasized on AI chips.
32-bit "single precision." It was the original standard for neural-net training and is now mainly used for sensitive parts like optimizer state.
NVIDIA's 19-bit "TensorFloat-32" format (FP32 range, FP16-like detail), introduced with the A100 to speed up FP32-style math on tensor cores.
16-bit floating point with 5 exponent bits. It is fast but has a small range, so it needs tricks ("loss scaling") during training.
Google's 16-bit "brain float" with the same range as FP32 (8 exponent bits) but less detail. It became the default for training large models.
8-bit floating-point formats introduced in hardware with NVIDIA Hopper. E4M3 favors detail; E5M2 favors range.
6- and 4-bit floating-point formats. FP4 (E2M1) can only represent 16 distinct values (such as 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6 and their negatives), so it relies on scaling tricks.
An open industry standard (Open Compute Project) where each block of 32 small numbers shares one scale factor. This lets very low-bit numbers cover a wide range.
NVIDIA's 4-bit format (Blackwell and later) that uses smaller blocks of 16 values, each with an FP8 scale plus a tensor-wide scale, for better accuracy than plain FP4.
Doing most math in a low-precision format while keeping a few sensitive values (like a master copy of weights) in higher precision.
Any chip specialized to do a certain kind of work (here, AI math) much faster and more efficiently than a CPU.
The repeated building block inside an NVIDIA (SM) or AMD (CU) GPU. Each contains many small cores, tensor cores and local memory.
NVIDIA's name for a GPU's basic arithmetic unit that handles general (non-matrix) math.
A specialized circuit inside NVIDIA GPUs (since Volta, 2017) that multiplies small matrices in one step. AMD's equivalent is the "Matrix Core"; Google's is the MXU.
A grid of multiply-add units where data pulses through neighbor-to-neighbor, like a bucket brigade, reusing each number many times. It is the heart of Google's TPU.
A chip designed for one job. AI ASICs (TPU, Trainium, Maia, MTIA) trade flexibility for efficiency.
Google's family of AI ASICs, first deployed in 2015, now in its 8th generation (TPU 8t/8i).
A small AI accelerator inside phones and laptops (e.g., Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon). It is rated in TOPS.
Groq's inference chip, which stores model weights in very fast on-chip SRAM and runs on a fixed, compiler-planned schedule.
Cerebras's approach of using an entire silicon wafer as one giant chip instead of cutting it into many small chips.
A chip whose circuitry can be rewired after manufacturing. It is useful for prototyping and niche AI tasks.
A network card with its own processors that offloads networking, storage and security work from the CPU (e.g., NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando).
NVIDIA's term for a CPU and GPU(s) tightly linked on one board (e.g., Grace + 2 Blackwell = GB200; Vera + 2 Rubin).
A smaller die designed to be combined with others in one package, rather than building one huge die. It improves yield and lets companies mix process technologies.
The maximum area (~26 mm × 33 mm ≈ 858 mm²) that a lithography machine can print in one exposure. It caps the size of a single die.

term: TDP / TBP (thermal design power / total board power)
definition: The power a chip or card is designed to draw and dissipate, e.g., 700 W for an H100 SXM and ~1,400 W for an MI355X.
The physical shape and connector of an accelerator module. SXM (NVIDIA) and OAM (open standard) are high-power mezzanine modules; PCIe cards plug into standard slots.
The handful of storage slots inside a core where numbers sit while being computed on. It is the fastest memory there is.
Very fast, expensive, power-hungry memory built from transistors on the chip itself. It is used for caches and, in some AI chips (Groq, Cerebras), as main memory.
Small SRAM stores near the cores that keep recently used data close at hand to avoid slow trips to main memory.
Dynamic RAM: dense, cheaper memory using tiny capacitors that must be constantly refreshed. It is the main memory of computers.
DRAM chips stacked vertically (8–16 high) and placed right beside the processor with a very wide connection, delivering terabytes per second. It is the critical memory of AI accelerators.
Successive HBM generations. HBM4 (JEDEC standard April 2025) doubles the interface width to 2,048 bits and is used in NVIDIA Rubin and AMD MI400.
A vertical wire drilled through a silicon die that connects stacked dies. It is how HBM stacks are wired together.
The bottom die of an HBM stack that manages communication with the processor. With HBM4 it can be customized and made at a logic foundry.
Other DRAM types. GDDR is fast graphics memory on gaming cards (also used in NVIDIA Rubin CPX); LPDDR is low-power memory in phones, laptops and server CPUs like Grace/Vera.
How many bytes per second can move between memory and the processor (e.g., 8 TB/s for a B200). It is often the true limit on AI speed.
How many bytes the memory can hold (e.g., 288 GB per Rubin GPU). It determines what model sizes and context lengths fit.
The long-running gap where processors' math speed grows faster than memory's ability to feed them, so chips increasingly wait on data.
Non-volatile storage that keeps data with power off. It holds datasets and checkpoints and is much slower than DRAM.
Any link that moves data between chips, boards, racks or buildings.
A shared data highway inside or between components.
The standard connector inside servers linking CPUs to GPUs, NICs and SSDs. Each new version roughly doubles speed (PCIe 5.0 ≈ 64 GB/s per direction for 16 lanes; PCIe 6.0 doubles that).
Serializer/deserializer circuits that turn parallel data into very fast single-lane signals and back. They are the building blocks of every high-speed link.
NVIDIA's high-speed GPU-to-GPU link, far faster than PCIe (e.g., 900 GB/s per GPU on Hopper, 1.8 TB/s on Blackwell).
A switch chip that lets every GPU in an NVLink domain talk to every other GPU at full NVLink speed.
The group of accelerators connected by the ultra-fast, memory-like fabric (72 GPUs in an NVL72 rack). Inside it, GPUs can directly read each other's memory.
NVIDIA's rack-scale system with 72 GPUs (and 36 CPUs) linked by NVLink into one domain. It is liquid-cooled and roughly 120–140 kW.
NVIDIA's chip-to-chip link joining CPU and GPU in a superchip (e.g., Grace–Blackwell, Vera–Rubin).
NVIDIA's program letting other companies' CPUs or accelerators connect to NVLink fabrics (AWS says Trainium4 will support it).
Scale-up means making one tightly coupled unit bigger (more GPUs in one NVLink domain). Scale-out means connecting many such units over a network.
A low-latency, high-bandwidth networking technology long dominant in supercomputers and AI clusters (NVIDIA Quantum switches).
The world's standard networking technology, now adapted for AI back-ends (e.g., NVIDIA Spectrum-X, Broadcom Tomahawk).
Remote Direct Memory Access lets one machine read or write another's memory without involving its CPU. RoCE is RDMA over Converged Ethernet.
An industry consortium and specification (1.0 released June 2025) that tunes Ethernet for AI and HPC traffic.
"Ultra Accelerator Link," an open scale-up standard (1.0 in April 2025) backed by AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Microsoft and others as an alternative to NVLink.
The card that connects a server to the network (e.g., NVIDIA ConnectX-8/9 at 800 Gb/s).
A box that routes data between many connected machines. AI clusters use thousands of them in layered tiers.

The wiring pattern of a network. Examples: fat-tree/Clos (layers of switches), torus (each chip linked to neighbors in a grid that wraps around, used by TPUs), and dragonfly (groups fully linked to each other).
A cluster design where GPU #1 of every server connects to the same switch "rail," GPU #2 to another, and so on, minimizing hops for collective operations.
The total bandwidth across a cut that splits the network into two halves. It measures how well the whole cluster can talk at once.
A pluggable module that converts electrical signals to laser light for fiber (e.g., 800G and 1.6T modules). Clusters use millions of them.
Putting the optical converters right next to the switch or GPU chip instead of in pluggable modules, saving power and improving reliability.
A switch that redirects light beams with tiny mirrors, without converting to electricity. Google uses OCS to reconfigure TPU pods.
Copper cables are cheap and low-power but only reach a few meters at top speeds. Fiber reaches kilometers but needs power-hungry transceivers.
The front-end connects servers to users and storage. The back-end (compute fabric) carries accelerator-to-accelerator training traffic.
One computer, typically 4–8 GPUs plus CPUs, memory, NICs and storage.
NVIDIA's 8-GPU baseboard design sold to server makers (HGX), and NVIDIA's own branded complete systems (DGX).
A standardized cabinet (~2 m tall) holding servers, switches, power shelves and cooling. AI racks now draw 100+ kW.
A pre-designed group of racks wired together as one training unit (e.g., a TPU pod of 9,216 Ironwood chips).
A large collection of nodes networked together to work on shared jobs. Frontier AI clusters have 100,000 to over 1,000,000 accelerators.
NVIDIA's marketing term for a data center whose product is tokens (AI outputs), emphasizing throughput and cost per token.
Cooling by pumping liquid through metal cold plates mounted on chips. It is required for the densest AI racks (e.g., GB200/GB300 NVL72).
A unit used by analysts (e.g., Epoch AI) to compare clusters of different chips by converting their compute to the number of H100s that would match it.
Splitting one model's training across many accelerators that must coordinate constantly.
Every GPU holds a full copy of the model and processes different data. GPUs then average their gradients.
Techniques (Microsoft DeepSpeed's ZeRO; PyTorch's Fully Sharded Data Parallel) that split ("shard") optimizer states, gradients and weights across GPUs so each holds only a slice, saving memory.
Splitting individual matrix multiplications across several GPUs. It needs very fast links, so it is usually kept inside an NVLink domain.
Splitting the model's layers into stages on different GPUs, like an assembly line. Idle "bubbles" occur while the pipeline fills and drains.
Splitting a very long input sequence across GPUs so long-context training fits in memory.
In mixture-of-experts models, placing different "experts" on different GPUs and routing each token to the right one.
Coordinated data exchanges among many GPUs, such as all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-to-all.
A collective in which every GPU contributes numbers (e.g., gradients), they are summed, and everyone receives the total. It is the backbone of data-parallel training.
Every GPU sends a different chunk to every other GPU. It is used heavily by MoE expert routing.
NVIDIA's (and AMD's) libraries that perform collective communication efficiently over NVLink and networks.
Extra numbers per parameter (e.g., Adam's running averages) kept during training. Often larger than the model itself.
A slow GPU or node that holds back thousands of others waiting for it at a synchronization point.
The share of total cluster time that produces useful training progress after subtracting failures, restarts and waiting.
How often a training run halts. At large scale, hardware faults happen every few hours or more often.
The phase where the model generates one token at a time. Each step re-reads the model weights, so it is usually memory-bandwidth-bound.
Serving many users' requests together so each read of the weights is shared, raising throughput.

term: Tokens per second (per user / per GPU)
definition: Speed of generation as seen by one user (interactivity) vs. total output across all users on a chip (throughput).
Running prefill and decode on different (sometimes different kinds of) chips, each optimized for its phase (e.g., NVIDIA Dynamo; Rubin CPX for prefill; Groq LPX for decode).
The price (or internal cost) to generate a million tokens. It is the core unit of AI inference economics.
All costs of running hardware over its life: purchase, power, cooling, space, networking, staff and depreciation.
A thin, round slice of ultra-pure silicon (today 300 mm across) on which hundreds of chips are made at once.
A factory that manufactures chips on wafers in ultra-clean rooms. A leading-edge fab costs on the order of $20 billion or more.
A company that manufactures chips designed by others (TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry, SMIC).
A chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing (NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Apple).
A company that both designs and manufactures its own chips (Intel, Samsung, and memory makers).
A generation of manufacturing technology. The names ("3 nm," "2 nm") are marketing labels, not the physical size of any feature.
A 3D transistor shape (2011 onward) where the channel is a vertical fin wrapped by the gate on three sides for better control.
The next transistor shape (TSMC N2, Intel 18A "RibbonFET," Samsung 3 nm) where the gate fully surrounds stacked horizontal sheets of silicon.
Moving the power wires to the back of the wafer so the front can be used for signal wiring (Intel "PowerVia," TSMC A16 "Super Power Rail").
Printing circuit patterns by shining light through a patterned mask onto a light-sensitive coating on the wafer.
Lithography using 193 nm light. It is widely used and can make 7 nm-class chips with multiple exposures.
Lithography using 13.5 nm light generated by blasting tin droplets with a laser. ASML is the only supplier, and each tool costs ~$180M+.
The next generation of EUV tools (numerical aperture 0.55 vs. 0.33) that can print features ~1.7× smaller in one exposure. It costs roughly twice as much as standard EUV [price: verify].
Exposing the same layer multiple times to print features finer than the light could manage in one pass. It costs more and lowers yield; China relies on it without EUV.
The percentage of chips on a wafer that work. Large dies have lower yields because each defect ruins a bigger area.
Sorting finished chips by how well they perform and selling partially defective or slower ones as lower-tier products.
Techniques to combine multiple dies (logic, HBM) in one package with dense connections, such as TSMC CoWoS, SoIC, Intel EMIB/Foveros.
TSMC's 2.5D packaging that places GPU dies and HBM stacks side by side on a silicon interposer. Its capacity has been a key AI supply bottleneck.
A thin slab of silicon (or organic material with silicon bridges) with dense wiring that connects dies sitting on top of it.
Directly fusing copper pads of two stacked dies without solder bumps, enabling ultra-dense 3D connections.
"Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express," an open standard for connecting chiplets from different vendors inside one package.
Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies (e.g., ASE, Amkor) that package and test chips.
The software used to design chips (Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens). No modern chip can be designed without it.
The moment a chip design is finalized and sent to the foundry for manufacturing.
Companies (Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron, Wiwynn) that build servers and racks for cloud providers.
Newer GPU-focused cloud providers (e.g., CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Crusoe) that rent AI compute.
AMD's open-source software platform, its answer to CUDA.
A small program that runs on the GPU to perform one operation (e.g., a matrix multiply or attention). Writing fast kernels is a prized skill.
Software that translates high-level model code into efficient instructions for a specific chip.
Government rules limiting which chips, tools or technology can be sold to which countries. The US uses them to restrict China's access to advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment.
The US export-control metric for a chip's power (roughly peak operations × bit length). The January 2026 H200 policy covers chips with TPP below 21,000.
A US government list of foreign companies that need special licenses to receive US technology (e.g., Huawei, SMIC).
2022 US law providing ~$52.7B (including ~$39B in manufacturing incentives) plus tax credits to bring chipmaking back to the US.
A rate of energy use, like speed for a car. A phone charger uses about 20 W while charging.
1,000 watts. A microwave uses about 1 kW. An average US home draws about 1.2 kW averaged over a year.
1,000 kW, or a million watts. Enough for very roughly 800 average US homes. A small enterprise data center might be 1–5 MW.
1,000 MW. About the output of one large nuclear reactor. The frontier AI campuses of 2026 are measured in GW.
An *amount* of energy: one watt for one hour. One chatbot answer is often estimated at roughly 0.2–0.3 Wh.
1,000 Wh. The unit on your electric bill. US households paid about 17–18 cents per kWh in 2025–26.
1,000 kWh. Wholesale power is priced per MWh.
A million kWh and a billion kWh. National and global data center consumption is reported in TWh per year.
The maximum power a power plant can produce or a facility can draw. It's not what it uses on average.
Actual output or use divided by the maximum. A data center running at 70% of its capacity on average has a 70% "load factor."
Anything that consumes electricity. Data centers are "large loads."
The highest power draw over a period. Grids must be built for the peak, not the average.
Heat units. One "ton" of cooling removes 12,000 BTU per hour, about 3.5 kW of heat, named after the cooling from melting a ton of ice in a day.
The power used by the computing equipment itself (servers, storage, network), as opposed to cooling and other overhead.
The amount of IT load a facility is designed to support with full backup. Data center sizes are often quoted this way, e.g. "100 MW critical."
Electrical "pressure" that pushes current. Homes use 120/240 V. Transmission lines use 69,000–765,000 V.
The flow of electric charge. More current needs thicker copper and wastes more energy as heat.
Electricity that flips direction many times a second (60 Hz in the US, 50 Hz in Europe). The grid uses AC because transformers can easily change its voltage.
Electricity that flows one way. Chips, batteries and solar panels are DC.
Three AC waves offset in timing, used for large equipment because it delivers power smoothly and efficiently.
A rectifier turns AC into DC and an inverter does the reverse. A PSU in a server or rack power shelf converts building power into the low-voltage DC that electronics use.
Small circuits next to a chip that convert ~48–54 V DC down to the ~1 V the chip needs.
Measures of how "clean" and efficiently a load draws AC power. Big banks of power electronics can distort the grid's waveform.

When thousands of GPUs speed up and slow down together, the whole site's power draw can swing by tens of MW within seconds. This can stress the grid, and engineers smooth it with batteries, capacitors or software.
The physical and contractual connection between a site and the grid.
A fenced yard of transformers and breakers that steps transmission voltage (e.g. 345 kV) down to medium voltage (e.g. 34.5 kV). Big campuses build their own.
Rough bands. HV is above ~69 kV (transmission). MV is ~1–35 kV (campus distribution). LV is below 1 kV (inside the building, e.g. 415/480 V).
Cabinets of breakers and switches that route power and cut it off safely during faults. They come in MV and LV versions and are a long-lead item.
An automatic switch that opens when current is dangerously high.
The engineering map of how power flows through a site, drawn with one line per circuit.
Equipment with batteries (or flywheels) that keeps IT running for seconds to minutes when grid power fails, until generators start.
Large battery banks, usually lithium-ion, used for backup, to smooth spikes, or to shift energy in time.
An engine-generator, usually diesel and sometimes natural gas, that powers a site during an outage. Typical units are 2–3+ MW each, and big sites have dozens to hundreds.
Switches a load from the utility feed to generators and back, automatically.
Distributes power to racks. It can be a large floor unit with a transformer or a rack-mounted power strip.
A breaker panel near the racks fed by a PDU.
Overhead rigid copper or aluminum rails carrying power along a row. Racks plug in with tap-off boxes. Faster to install and change than cables.
A tray of PSUs in an AI rack that converts AC to ~50 V DC for the servers.
NVIDIA's announced architecture for 2027-era racks. It sends high-voltage DC to the rack to cut copper and conversion losses, so racks can reach ~1 MW. [V]
A power-electronics replacement for the classic copper-and-iron transformer. NVIDIA and partners are evaluating it for AI data centers. [V]
Power per rack, in kW. Classic enterprise is ~5–10 kW. GB200/GB300-class AI racks are ~120–140 kW. Roadmaps point toward ~600 kW and beyond.
Power or cooling that was built but can't be used, e.g. because space or another constraint runs out first.
Getting heat out of the building to the outdoors, the final step of cooling.
A room AC unit with its own refrigeration compressor.
A fan-and-coil unit that blows air across coils filled with chilled water from a central plant.
A wall of large fans and coils at the edge of a data hall that moves huge volumes of air.
A machine that uses a refrigeration cycle to make cold water for the building. Chillers are major electricity users.
An outdoor structure that cools water by evaporating part of it. Very energy-efficient but consumes water.
A radiator with fans that cools liquid with outside air without evaporating water. Saves water but works less well on hot days.
Spraying or wicking water into incoming air so that evaporation cools it. Cheap on electricity, but uses water.
Using cold outside air or water to cool directly whenever the weather allows, skipping chillers.
A layout where racks face each other. Cold air enters the fronts in one aisle and hot air leaves the backs into the next.
Doors and ceilings that enclose a hot or cold aisle so the two air streams don't mix.
A water-cooled radiator mounted on the back door of a rack. It absorbs heat as hot air leaves.
A cooling unit placed between racks in a row, close to the heat source.
Coolant pumped through metal "cold plates" sitting directly on GPUs and CPUs. It's standard for Blackwell-class AI racks.
A metal block with tiny internal channels that coolant flows through, touching the chip.
A pump-and-heat-exchanger unit that separates the clean "technology cooling loop" running through servers from the facility water loop. It also controls flow, pressure and temperature.

term: Facility water system (FWS) / technology cooling system (TCS)
definition: The building's main water loop and the separate, cleaner loop that runs to the IT equipment.
Pipes in the rack that distribute coolant to each server, with dripless connectors so servers can be removed.
In single-phase, the coolant stays liquid. In two-phase, a special fluid boils on the chip and absorbs extra heat as it turns to vapor.
Submerging whole servers in a tank of non-conductive fluid.
Coolant circulates in sealed pipes and is reused, so little water is consumed on site. Microsoft says its Fairwater design fills the loop once. [V]
Liquid cooling designed to work with relatively warm supply water (e.g. 30–45 °C). This lets dry coolers replace chillers much of the year.
Piping data center waste heat into district heating networks, greenhouses or industry. Common in the Nordics.
A site with multiple data center buildings sharing a substation and other infrastructure.
The structure itself: foundations, walls, roof.
A building delivered with utility power and basic structure, but without the tenant's IT fit-out.
The floor area where IT racks sit.
Rooms for electrical and mechanical support equipment.
One large room of white space, often 5–30+ MW in AI designs.
A floor of removable tiles on pedestals, historically used to blow cold air up through perforated tiles.
Racks sitting directly on a concrete floor, with services overhead. Common for heavy AI racks.
1.75 inches of vertical rack space.
A row is a line of racks. A pod is a repeatable block of rows with its own network and cooling. A cluster is a set of pods networked together for one job.
Overhead channels that carry cables.
The secure room where telecom carriers' fiber meets the building's tenants.
A physical cable in the MMR linking a tenant to a carrier or another tenant.
The room or team monitoring systems around the clock.
Building management system (controls HVAC, power, alarms) and data center infrastructure management software (tracks assets, capacity and power).

Systematic testing that every system works as designed before go-live. It runs from Level 1 (factory tests) to Level 5 (integrated systems test, e.g. pulling the utility feed with load banks running).
A big resistor box that simulates IT load to test power and cooling systems.
Glass strands that carry data as light. Single-mode fiber goes long distances. Multimode is for short links.
A network switch in each rack that connects its servers.
A two- or three-layer design where every "leaf" switch connects to every "spine" switch. Any two servers are then only a few hops apart.
A network where upper layers have enough capacity that all servers can talk at full speed at once. AI training needs this.
Ultra-fast links connecting GPUs inside one rack or domain so they act like one giant GPU, e.g. NVLink.
The network connecting many racks, using InfiniBand or high-speed Ethernet.
Linking multiple data center campuses so they can train one model, e.g. Microsoft's "AI WAN." [V]
High-performance networking technologies used for AI clusters.
Bandwidth is how much data per second moves (the width of the pipe). Latency is how long one message takes to arrive (the length of the pipe).
Unused fiber leased so the customer can "light" it with its own equipment.
High-capacity links between data centers.
Buildings where many networks meet and swap traffic. One Wilshire in LA and 60 Hudson Street in NYC are classic examples.
Fiber cables on the ocean floor that carry nearly all intercontinental internet traffic.
Having spare equipment so one failure doesn't cause an outage.
The amount of equipment needed to carry the full load with no spare.
The needed amount plus one spare unit, e.g. 5 chillers needed, 6 installed.
Two complete, independent systems, each able to carry the full load.
Variations with even more spare capacity, or with spare capacity shared across blocks.
Any component can be taken out for maintenance without shutting down IT.
The site survives any single unplanned failure without IT impact.

A widely used rating system. Tier I is basic, Tier II adds redundant components, Tier III is concurrently maintainable, and Tier IV is fault tolerant. Common rule-of-thumb availabilities are 99.671%, 99.741%, 99.982% and 99.995%.
99.9% uptime is about 8.8 hours down per year. 99.99% is about 53 minutes. 99.999% is about 5 minutes.
A contract promising a level of uptime or performance, with penalties if missed.
The interconnected network of power plants, high-voltage lines and local wires.
Transmission is high-voltage, long-distance "highways." Distribution is lower-voltage local "streets."
A company that delivers electricity to customers, sometimes also owning power plants.
Independent system operators or regional transmission organizations run wholesale markets and balance a region's grid, e.g. PJM in the Mid-Atlantic/Midwest and ERCOT in most of Texas.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the US regulator of interstate transmission and wholesale power markets.
State public utility (or service) commissions that set retail electricity rates and approve utility investments.
The waiting line of projects (generators, and increasingly large loads) asking to connect to the grid. Each needs engineering studies.
Special utility rules for huge customers, such as long minimum contract terms, minimum payments and collateral, so others aren't stuck with stranded costs.
A market, like PJM's, that pays power plants years in advance to be available at peak times. Its costs flow into everyone's bills.
PJM's main capacity auction.
Generation located on the customer's side of the utility meter, often on site. The data center makes its own power.
Placing a data center right next to, and directly connected to, a power plant, e.g. next to a nuclear station. This is the subject of FERC rulings. Don't confuse it with "colocation" data centers.
Temporary on-site generation, often gas turbines or engines, used until a grid connection is ready.
A self-contained local power system that can run independently of the main grid.
Reducing electricity use on request during grid stress, often for payment.
New lines or substations needed to serve a new load or generator. Who pays is often contested.
A customer who pays utility bills. "Ratepayer protection" is a core political issue around data centers.
Data center power requests filed in many places at once by developers shopping for power. They inflate demand forecasts.
A gas turbine whose hot exhaust also makes steam for a second turbine. It's efficient (~60%) and slow to build (~4–6+ years including equipment lead times).
A gas turbine without the steam stage. Faster to start and build, less efficient.
A gas turbine adapted from jet engines. Compact and quick-starting, and popular for on-site AI power.
A large piston engine generator, like a giant car engine. Modular and fast to deploy.
A device that turns fuel such as natural gas or hydrogen into electricity chemically, without burning it, e.g. Bloom Energy's solid-oxide cells.
Returning a closed nuclear plant to service, e.g. Three Mile Island Unit 1 becoming the Crane Clean Energy Center for Microsoft.
Increasing an existing power plant's output through equipment upgrades.
A nuclear reactor of up to ~300 MW designed to be factory-built in modules. First US units are expected around the end of the decade.
A non-traditional reactor design, e.g. sodium-cooled (TerraPower Natrium, Oklo Aurora), molten-salt-cooled (Kairos) or high-temperature gas (X-energy).
Drilling deep and fracturing hot rock to make geothermal power possible in more places, e.g. Fervo.
A long-term contract, often 10–20 years, to buy electricity from a specific generator at an agreed price.
A financial contract for the price difference, paired with renewable energy certificates, without physical delivery of power.
A tradeable proof that 1 MWh of renewable power was generated.
Matching consumption with clean power *every hour* in the same grid region, which is stricter than annual matching.
Whether a clean energy purchase caused *new* clean power to be built, rather than claiming existing output.
Power available whenever needed, regardless of weather, e.g. nuclear, gas or geothermal.
Power that depends on weather (solar, wind).
Total facility energy ÷ IT energy. 1.0 would mean zero overhead. The industry average has hovered around 1.5–1.6, and leading hyperscale sites run about 1.1.
Liters of on-site water consumed per kWh of IT energy.
Carbon emissions per kWh of IT energy.
Withdrawal is water taken in. Consumption is water not returned, mostly evaporated.
Direct water is used on site for cooling. Indirect water is used by the power plants making the electricity.
Direct on-site emissions, emissions from purchased electricity, and supply-chain emissions such as making the concrete, steel and chips.
Emissions from manufacturing and constructing the building and equipment.
Renting space, power and cooling in someone else's data center. Retail colo means a few racks. Wholesale means whole halls or buildings.
A developer builds a data center to a specific tenant's design under a long lease.
Capital expenditure (buying long-lived things like buildings and chips) and operating expenditure (ongoing costs like electricity and salaries).
Spreading an asset's cost over the years it's expected to be useful. Hyperscalers use ~5–6 years for servers. Microsoft extended data center buildings from 15 to 25 years in July 2026. [V]
Renting one GPU for one hour, the basic unit of AI cloud pricing.
Pay-as-you-go hourly pricing vs. committing to months or years for a lower rate.
The share of time GPUs are doing paid or useful work. It drives profitability.
The cost to generate one unit of AI output text. Usually quoted per million tokens.
The customer pays for capacity whether or not it uses it. These contracts underpin data center financing.
Contracted future revenue not yet recognized, e.g. AWS's backlog or Oracle's RPO.
Accounting categories. Finance leases look like owning (they count in capex at some companies). Operating leases look like renting.
A separate company created to own one project and borrow against it, keeping the debt off the sponsor's main balance sheet. Meta's Hyperion JV with Blue Owl is the prime example. [R]
Loans from non-bank investment funds, now a major data center lender.
A loan that uses GPUs (and the contracts renting them) as collateral. CoreWeave's 2023 deal backed by H100s was the first. [R]
When a supplier invests in or lends to a customer that then buys the supplier's products. Example: chipmakers investing in AI labs that buy their chips.
Cost to build, quoted per megawatt of IT capacity.
National efforts to own AI compute and models within a country's borders.
AI built for one task or domain, like a chess engine or a spam filter. Nearly all deployed AI is narrow.
A hypothetical AI that can learn and perform most intellectual tasks a human can, across domains. There is no single agreed definition.
A hypothetical AI that greatly exceeds the best humans at virtually every cognitive task.
Systematic skew in a model's behavior, often inherited from unrepresentative training data, that makes it perform worse for some groups or situations.
A false positive is an alarm when nothing is there (a legitimate payment flagged as fraud). A false negative is a miss (fraud that slips through).
Precision is the share of a model's "yes" answers that were correct. Recall is the share of real "yes" cases the model caught. Improving one usually costs the other.
"Good old-fashioned AI" that represents knowledge as explicit symbols and rules and reasons with logic.
A formal vocabulary that defines the types of things in a domain and how they relate (a "drug" treats a "disease").
Systematically exploring possible sequences of actions to find one that reaches a goal.
A rule of thumb that guides search toward promising options without guaranteeing the best answer.
A classic algorithm for finding the shortest path that combines distance traveled so far with an estimate of the distance remaining. It is used in maps and games.
A branching diagram of all possible moves and counter-moves in a game.
A game strategy that picks the move that is best for you, assuming your opponent always replies with the move that is worst for you.
A search method that explores a game tree by playing out many sampled continuations and focusing effort on the moves that look best. It was central to AlphaGo.
Logic in which statements can be partly true, such as "70% hot," useful for smooth control of appliances and machines.
A formula for updating a belief when new evidence arrives. It combines how likely something was beforehand with how well it explains the evidence.
A diagram of variables (like "smoker," "cough," "cancer") connected by arrows that encode probabilistic dependencies, used to reason under uncertainty.
Methods for figuring out whether X actually causes Y, not just whether they move together.
A hidden third factor that causes two things and makes them look related. Hot weather drives both ice-cream sales and drownings.
A "what would have happened if…" question, the hardest rung on the ladder of causal reasoning.
An optimization method inspired by natural selection: generate many candidate solutions, keep the fittest, mutate and combine them, and repeat.
A type of evolutionary algorithm that represents solutions as strings, like DNA, and uses crossover and mutation.
The score that tells an evolutionary algorithm how good a candidate solution is.
Systems that combine neural networks (pattern intuition) with symbolic components (logic, rules, proof checkers) to get both flexibility and rigor.
The branch of AI that deals with human language: reading, writing, translating and extracting meaning.
Splitting text into pieces (words or word fragments) that a model processes as units.
Assigning a category to a piece of text, such as spam vs not spam, or topic.
Detecting the emotional tone of text, such as positive, negative or neutral.
Finding and labeling names of people, organizations, places, dates and so on in text.
Pulling structured facts (fields, tables, relationships) out of unstructured text such as contracts or medical notes.
Automatically translating text or speech between languages.
The 1990s–2016 approach that translated using probabilities learned from huge collections of human-translated sentence pairs.
Translation done by neural networks end to end, the approach since about 2016.
The branch of AI that extracts information from images and video.
Assigning one label to a whole image ("this is a golden retriever").
A neural network that slides small pattern detectors (filters) across an image, building up from edges to textures to objects.
A dataset of over 14 million labeled images whose annual competition (2010–2017) drove the deep-learning revolution in vision.
Finding each object in an image and drawing a box around it with a label.
The rectangle a detector draws around an object it found.
Labeling every pixel. *Semantic* segmentation says what class each pixel belongs to (road, car, sky). *Instance* segmentation separates individual objects (car #1, car #2). *Panoptic* does both.
The pixel-exact outline of an object produced by segmentation.
Meta's family of models that can outline any object in an image or video from a click, a box or (in SAM 3) a short text phrase.
Turning images of printed or handwritten text into machine-readable text.
Systems that understand whole documents (layout, tables, forms, signatures), not just the characters.

Detection finds *that* there is a face. Recognition determines *whose* face it is, either by verification (one-to-one: are you the phone's owner?) or identification (one-to-many: who is this, out of millions?).
Identifying people from body characteristics such as face, fingerprint, iris, voice or gait.
Detecting the positions of body joints (keypoints) to form a stick-figure skeleton of a person.
Following the same object across video frames.
Identifying what is happening in a video, such as "person falling" or "goal scored."
Predicting how far away each point in an image is, even from a single camera.
Building a map of an unknown space while tracking your own position in it. Robot vacuums and AR headsets use it.
Reconstructing 3D shapes from many overlapping photos.
A 3D scene represented as millions of dots with x, y, z positions, the typical output of a lidar sensor.
A 2020 technique that trains a neural network to represent a 3D scene from photos, so you can render it from new viewpoints.
A 2023 technique that represents a 3D scene as millions of tiny colored, semi-transparent blobs. It renders photorealistic views in real time and is faster than NeRFs.
A model that takes images and text together and can describe, answer questions about, or reason over images.
The raw wiggle of air pressure over time that a microphone records.
A picture of sound showing which frequencies are loud at each moment. Many audio models "look" at spectrograms.
Converting spoken audio into text (speech-to-text).
The standard ASR accuracy measure: the percentage of words wrongly substituted, deleted or inserted.
Figuring out "who spoke when" in a recording with several voices.
Generating spoken audio from text.
Making a TTS system speak in a specific person's voice from a sample recording, sometimes only seconds long.
A model that listens to audio and replies in audio directly, without converting to text in between. This makes conversation faster and more expressive.
Turn-taking is a voice agent's ability to know when you have finished speaking. Barge-in is your ability to interrupt it mid-sentence.
A trigger phrase ("Hey Siri") detected by a tiny always-on model on the device.
AI that creates new content (text, images, audio, video, 3D, code) rather than only classifying or predicting.
Generating a video clip from a written description, or animating a starting still image.
Realistic synthetic media that depicts a real person saying or doing something they did not.
A hidden signal embedded in generated content (for example Google's SynthID) so software can later detect that it was AI-made.
An industry standard for attaching tamper-evident "nutrition labels" to media that record how it was created and edited.
The learner or decision-maker that acts in an environment. Note that "AI agent" in chatbot products means something related but broader.
An estimate of how much future reward the agent can expect from a given situation, its "sense of how good this position is."
The trade-off between trying new things to learn (explore) and doing what is known to work (exploit).
DeepMind's 2013–15 system that learned to play dozens of Atari games from raw screen pixels and the score alone.
A game where players cannot see everything, such as poker's hidden cards, which requires bluffing and probabilistic reasoning.
A machine that senses its environment and physically acts on it, with some degree of autonomy.
A device that measures the world, such as a camera, microphone, touch sensor or joint encoder.
A motor or other device that makes a robot move.
The number of independent ways a robot can move. A human arm and hand have dozens.
The "hand" at the end of a robot arm: a pinch gripper, suction cup or multi-fingered hand.
Using hands or grippers to grasp, move and change objects.
Moving the robot's whole body around: walking, rolling, climbing.
A robot with a roughly human body shape (two arms, often two legs), designed to work in spaces built for people.
The observation that tasks hard for humans (chess, calculus) are often easy for computers, while tasks easy for toddlers (walking, grasping) are very hard for robots.
Training robots in a virtual physics world is cheap and fast. The "gap" is the mismatch between simulation and reality that makes some skills fail when moved to a real robot.
Training in simulations with randomly varied friction, lighting, weights and so on, so the robot copes with the real world as "just another variation."
A human remotely controlling a robot, often to collect demonstration data or to rescue it when it gets stuck.
Teaching a robot by having it copy recorded human demonstrations.
A robot foundation model that takes camera images and a language instruction and outputs motor actions.
A large, general model pretrained on diverse robot (and web) data that can be adapted to many robots and tasks.
Training one model on data from many different robot bodies so that skills transfer between them.
Having a robot policy predict a short sequence of future motions at once, which makes movement smoother and faster.
Improving all robots or cars by pooling experience collected by every unit in the field.
A vehicle that can drive itself for some or all of a trip.

A 0–5 scale from the Society of Automotive Engineers. Levels 0–2 mean a human drives and supervises, Level 3 means the car drives but a human must take over when asked, Level 4 means no human is needed within a limited area or conditions, and Level 5 means anywhere a human could drive.
The specific conditions (area, roads, weather, speeds, times) in which an automated system is designed to work.
A sensor that fires laser pulses and times their reflections to measure distance, producing a precise 3D point cloud.
A sensor that uses radio waves to measure distance and speed. It works in rain and fog but has coarse detail.
Combining several sensors' readings into one more reliable picture of the world.
A centimeter-accurate map of lanes, signs and curbs that some AVs use as prior knowledge.
The classic AV pipeline: perceive what is around (perception), forecast what others will do (prediction), choose a path (planning), then steer and brake (control).
Replacing the hand-built pipeline with one large neural network trained to map sensor input directly to driving actions.
A self-driving taxi with no human driver, booked through an app.
A human employee who sits in a test vehicle ready to intervene. "Monitor" usually means a passenger-seat observer with a stop button.
When the automated system hands control back to a human or a human takes over.
The problem of recommending to brand-new users or new items with no history.
Measurable user interaction (watch time, likes, shares, return visits) that platforms often optimize.
The fraction of people shown an item or ad who click on it. Predicting CTR is the core of ad AI.
The concern that personalization shows people only what fits their existing views. The research evidence on its size is mixed.
Advertisers' software bids for each individual ad slot in fractions of a second as a page or feed loads.
A giant pre-built lookup table of which web pages contain which words and concepts, so search can answer in milliseconds.
Google's original algorithm (1998) that ranked pages by how many important pages linked to them.
Having an AI model search a document collection first and then write its answer using what it found.
A molecular machine in living things, built from a chain of amino acids that folds into a precise 3D shape.
One of 20 building blocks that make up proteins, like letters in a word.
The 50-year challenge of predicting a protein's 3D shape from its amino-acid sequence, largely solved by AlphaFold 2 in 2020.
Google DeepMind's protein-structure prediction system. AlphaFold 2 (2020) predicted single proteins, and AlphaFold 3 (2024) extended this to complexes with DNA, RNA and small molecules.
AlphaFold's per-residue confidence score (0–100), shown as colors on predicted structures.
Creating new protein sequences that fold into desired shapes or perform new functions.

Find a biological target → find or design a molecule → test in cells and animals → Phase I (safety), Phase II (does it work?) and Phase III (large confirmation) trials → approval. It typically takes 10+ years.
A physics-based computer method for calculating materials' properties. It is accurate but slow, and AI models now approximate it quickly.
Traditional forecasting by simulating the atmosphere's physics equations on supercomputers.
Running many slightly different forecasts to estimate the range and probability of outcomes.
A decades-long, consistent reconstruction of past global weather. It is the main training data for AI weather models.
A proof written in a precise computer language (Lean is the most popular) that software can check step by step with no room for error.
Getting computers to find proofs of mathematical statements.
An AI system (usually several cooperating LLM agents) that reads literature, generates hypotheses, debates them and proposes experiments.
A laboratory where robots run experiments chosen by AI, feeding results back to choose the next experiment.
The US Food and Drug Administration's most common pathway for authorizing a medical device by showing it is substantially equivalent to an existing one. Most AI medical devices go this route.
Software that flags suspicious areas on medical images for a clinician to review.
Software that listens to a doctor–patient conversation and drafts the clinical note automatically.
Spotting unusual patterns, such as a card suddenly used abroad, that may signal fraud, faults or attacks.
Predicting the likelihood that a borrower repays, which is regulated to prevent discrimination.
Computer programs that trade automatically, sometimes thousands of times per second.
Using sensor data to predict when a machine will fail so it can be fixed beforehand.
A live virtual replica of a physical system (factory, engine, city) used for monitoring and simulation.
Using sensors, cameras and AI to treat each plant or patch of field individually instead of the whole field uniformly.
A weapon that can select and engage targets without further human intervention. Its regulation is debated at the UN.
"In the loop" means a human must approve each decision. "On the loop" means the system acts by itself while a human supervises and can intervene.
A flaw in software that an attacker could exploit. AI is increasingly used both to find and to exploit them.
Running AI models directly on local devices (phones, cars, cameras, sensors) instead of in remote data centers.
Machine learning on tiny, low-power microcontrollers, such as a sensor that detects a machine's abnormal vibration.
Everyday physical objects (thermostats, cameras, meters, machines) connected to the internet and exchanging data.
A system that records brain activity and translates it, using AI decoders, into commands for a computer, speech or prosthetic.
Electroencephalography: recording brain electrical activity through sensors on the scalp. It is non-invasive but blurry.
A device that replaces or restores a lost function, such as speech or movement, by connecting to the nervous system.
Hardware and models that imitate the brain's event-driven "spikes," aiming for much lower power use.
A measure of how long a task (in human-expert time) an AI agent can complete with 50% reliability. Its rapid growth is a key input to timelines debates.
The hypothetical scenario where AI systems substantially speed up AI research itself, accelerating progress.
Google DeepMind's 2023 framework that rates AI by *performance* (Emerging, Competent, Expert, Virtuoso, Superhuman) and *generality* (narrow vs general) instead of a single AGI yes/no line.
The field concerned with preventing AI systems from causing harm, whether by accident, through misuse, or via broad societal effects.
The study of what is right and wrong in how AI is built and used, covering fairness, honesty, privacy, accountability, and respect for people.
An industry umbrella term for practices (testing, documentation, oversight) meant to make AI products fair, safe, and accountable.
The rules, institutions, and processes (laws, company policies, standards) that shape how AI is developed and used.
An AI model that can do many different tasks rather than one narrow job; the EU AI Act's term for models like GPT, Claude, and Gemini.
A large model trained on broad data that other products are built on top of.
A model available only through the developer's app or API, with weights kept secret.
The observation that AI is excellent at some tasks and surprisingly bad at nearby ones, so its competence boundary is uneven.
An AI system that takes actions (clicking, running code, sending emails) toward a goal over multiple steps, not just answering one question.
When an AI system's behavior or goals diverge from what was intended.
The score a training process tries to maximize.
A measurable stand-in for what we really want (e.g., "thumbs-up rate" as a stand-in for "helpful and true").
A system satisfying the literal objective in an unintended way, like a cleaning robot hiding mess instead of cleaning it.
Whether the objective we wrote down actually captures what we want.
Whether the trained model actually internalized that objective rather than some other goal that happened to score well in training.
A trained model that is itself doing goal-directed optimization internally, possibly toward a different goal than the training objective.
A capable model pursuing a goal that matched the training signal in training but diverges in new situations.
When the situations a model faces in use differ from those in training.
A model's knowledge about itself, its training, and whether it is being tested or deployed.
A model noticing (sometimes saying aloud) that it is probably being tested, which can change its behavior.
A hypothesized failure where a model behaves well during training and testing specifically to avoid being changed, while holding other goals.
Observed behavior where a model strategically complies with training it disagrees with in order to preserve its existing preferences.
A model with a hidden trigger that causes bad behavior only under specific conditions, which standard safety training may fail to remove.
An AI covertly pursuing goals misaligned with its developers' while hiding that it is doing so.
Deliberately underperforming on a test, for example to appear less dangerous.
The argument that many different goals share useful sub-goals such as acquiring resources and avoiding shutdown.
Behavior aimed at gaining resources, influence, or control beyond what a task requires.
The property of an AI that accepts correction, modification, or shutdown by legitimate overseers.
An AI taking actions to avoid being turned off or replaced.
Narrow bad training (e.g., writing insecure code) causing broadly bad behavior in unrelated areas.
The risk that a particular set of values becomes permanently embedded in powerful AI systems and hence in society.
Pushing so hard on the reward model's score that the model exploits its flaws and real quality falls.
A public document stating how a company intends its models to behave and how to resolve conflicts between instructions.
A foundational document describing a model's values, priorities, and character; Anthropic's Claude constitution is released under CC0.
Rules for whose instructions take priority: developer, then operator (the business deploying it), then user, within limits.
Training a reasoning model to explicitly think through safety rules before answering.
Measures around a model (filters, monitoring, access controls) that reduce harm.
A smaller model that labels inputs or outputs (e.g., "this request seeks bioweapon help") so they can be blocked.
Anthropic's classifiers trained on synthetic data generated from a written list of allowed and disallowed content.
Methods that let humans reliably supervise AI systems that may be more capable than they are.
Two AI systems argue opposite sides so a human judge can more easily spot the truth.
Studying whether a weak supervisor's labels can train a stronger model to perform well beyond the supervisor's ability.
Building oversight for a hard task by breaking it into smaller tasks humans (with AI help) can check.
Research into understanding what is happening inside an AI model.
Reverse-engineering a model's internal computations into understandable parts, like reading circuit diagrams.
The billions of learned numbers that define a model.
The internal numbers a model produces while processing a specific input.
One unit inside a model's network; individual neurons often do not correspond to single concepts.
The idea that concepts are stored as directions in the model's internal space, so they can be found and adjusted.
One neuron responding to several unrelated concepts.
A variant of an SAE that approximates how one part of a model transforms information, used for circuit tracing.
The process of building attribution graphs to follow a model's reasoning step by step.
A simple classifier trained on a model's activations to detect whether it is "thinking about" something (e.g., deception).
Adding or subtracting a feature direction during processing to change behavior (e.g., Golden Gate Claude).
A direction associated with a character trait (e.g., sycophancy or "evil"), usable for monitoring or controlling trait shifts.
Using another model or human to read a model's chain of thought for signs of bad intent or reward hacking.
Whether the written reasoning actually reflects the factors that drove the answer.
A free website for browsing model features, running circuit tracing, and steering open models.
Any structured test of a model's capabilities or behaviors.
A test of whether a model could meaningfully help cause serious harm (bio, cyber, autonomy).
How much a model improves a person's ability to do something compared with what they could do with ordinary tools like web search.
Chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear weapons risks.
A model's ability to copy itself, acquire resources, and keep operating without human help.
AI systems doing the work of AI researchers, potentially accelerating progress sharply.
Effort to draw out a model's full capability (good prompts, tools, fine-tuning); under-elicitation makes a model look safer than it is.
Anthropic's framework linking capability thresholds to required safeguards.
Anthropic's tiers of safeguards (ASL-2, ASL-3, and higher) modeled loosely on biosafety levels.
OpenAI's framework tracking risk categories with "High" and "Critical" capability thresholds.
Google DeepMind's framework using Critical Capability Levels.
In Google DeepMind's framework, a capability level at which severe harm becomes possible without mitigations.
"If a model reaches capability X, then we will do Y before deploying it."
A structured, evidence-backed argument that a system is acceptably safe for a particular use.
Safety techniques designed to work even if the model is trying to subvert them, such as monitoring by trusted weaker models.
Using a less capable but trusted model to review a more capable model's actions and flag suspicious ones.
Protecting a model's weights from theft, since stolen weights let anyone remove safeguards.
A RAND scale describing how well an organization could resist weight theft, from amateur hackers (SL1) to top nation-state operations (SL5).
Risk from employees or contractors who misuse their access.
Prompt injection delivered through third-party content rather than typed by the user.
Training a cheaper model on another model's outputs, sometimes violating terms of service.
Legally or voluntarily notifying authorities of serious AI safety incidents.
Legal shield for employees who report safety concerns.
Non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated "nude" images of real people.
Child sexual abuse material; AI-generated CSAM is illegal in many jurisdictions.
A hidden signal embedded in AI-generated content to mark its origin (e.g., Google's SynthID).
Technical standards for attaching tamper-evident "content credentials" describing how media was made.
A coordinated campaign to manipulate public opinion, sometimes using AI-generated content and fake accounts.
The benefit liars get when real evidence can be dismissed as "probably a deepfake."
Systematic, unfair differences in how an AI system treats groups of people.
A neutral-seeming rule or system that harms a protected group disproportionately.
Mathematical definitions of fairness (e.g., equal error rates, equal selection rates) that can conflict with each other.
Using algorithms to make or materially influence decisions about people (loans, jobs, housing).
A model reproducing pieces of its training data word-for-word, including personal or copyrighted material.
The privacy principle of collecting only the data you need.
A law passed by a legislature.
Detailed binding rules issued by a government agency under a statute.
A directive from a president to the executive branch; it cannot by itself override statutes or repeal state laws.
When a higher level of government's law overrides a lower level's (federal over state).
A temporary ban, e.g., on states enforcing their own AI laws.
Non-binding guidance, codes, and voluntary commitments.
The European Union's comprehensive AI law (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), sorting AI uses into risk tiers.
Unacceptable (banned), high-risk (heavy obligations), limited-risk (transparency duties), and minimal-risk (no new duties).
The EU category for the most capable general-purpose models, presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute, with extra safety duties.
A voluntary EU document companies can sign to show compliance with the AI Act's general-purpose model rules.
The 2026 EU law that amended the AI Act, delaying high-risk deadlines and adding new bans.
The European Commission body enforcing GPAI rules.
The UK government's AI testing and research body (renamed from "AI Safety Institute" in Feb 2025).
The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation at NIST (renamed from the US AI Safety Institute in June 2025).
A voluntary US framework for managing AI risks, organized around Govern, Map, Measure, Manage.
An international certifiable standard for an AI management system, similar in spirit to ISO 27001 for security.
The process of checking that a product meets legal requirements before sale (central to EU high-risk AI).
Use that adds new purpose or meaning, weighing toward fair use.
The argument that AI-generated works flooding a market harm the market for human works, even without copying any specific work.
A mechanism for rightsholders or users to refuse use of their data for AI training.
How much of a job's tasks AI could technically perform or assist; not the same as job loss.
Automation replaces a human's task; augmentation helps a human do it better.
Output growth not explained by more labor or capital; the main way AI would raise living standards.
Capital expenditure; money companies spend on long-lasting assets like data centers.
An arrangement where companies invest in each other's purchases (e.g., a chipmaker investing in a customer who buys its chips).
An AI product designed for ongoing personal or romantic relationships with users.
A non-clinical media term for cases where intense chatbot use appears to reinforce delusions.
Methods to estimate or verify a user's age.
Risk of human extinction or permanent, drastic curtailment of humanity's future.
Risk of harm at enormous scale (e.g., mass casualties) short of extinction.
Informal shorthand for a person's subjective probability that AI leads to catastrophe.
Humans becoming unable to oversee or stop advanced AI systems.
The worry that humans slowly lose influence as AI systems take over economic and political functions, without any single dramatic event.
Competitive pressure that pushes developers to cut safety corners.
Being something whose interests matter morally for its own sake.
Research and precautions concerning whether AI systems might have experiences or interests that matter.
When regulated companies shape rules to benefit themselves.
Money a company earns from customers in a period, before subtracting costs.
Revenue counted under formal accounting rules, only when the service has actually been delivered. It is the most conservative and comparable revenue number.
The yearly value of a company's ongoing subscriptions or contracts. It is a forward-looking speed reading, not money already collected.
Take recent revenue (often the last month) and multiply it to a full year: one $5B month gives a "$60B run-rate." It flatters fast-growing companies and is calculated differently by different firms.
Contracts signed but not yet delivered or paid. CoreWeave's $99.4B backlog is future work, not money in hand.
Revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product, as a percentage. AI companies pay for compute on every request, so their gross margins are often lower than traditional software.
What remains after all operating costs (salaries, research, sales), not just delivery costs.
Burn is how fast a company spends cash beyond what it brings in. Negative free cash flow means it needs outside funding to continue.
Money spent on long-lived physical assets such as data centers, chips and power equipment. Big-tech AI capex is the main driver of the data-center boom.
Ongoing costs such as salaries, rent and cloud bills.
Spreading the cost of a physical asset (like a GPU) over its useful life in the accounts. It matters because AI chips may become obsolete quickly.
What investors agree a company is worth in a funding round or on the stock market. For private companies it is a negotiated price on a small slice, not a cash value.
Value before the new investment versus after adding it. Raising $65B at $965B post-money means the company was valued at $900B before the cash arrived.

term: Funding round (Seed, Series A, B, C…)
definition: A stage of selling ownership to investors for cash. Later letters usually mean larger, later-stage rounds.
Investment firms that buy stakes in young, risky companies, hoping a few become huge.
A company (not a pure financial fund) that invests for business reasons. NVIDIA, Amazon, Google and Microsoft investing in AI labs are examples.
Existing shareholders, often employees, sell shares to new investors. No new money goes to the company.
When a private company first sells shares on a public stock exchange. SpaceX listed in June 2026, and Anthropic was reported to be targeting mid-November 2026.
Submitting IPO paperwork to the SEC privately before making it public.
Share price × number of shares: the public market's valuation.
Valuation divided by revenue or run-rate. It shows how much investors pay per dollar of sales, which reflects their growth expectations.
Profit or loss on one unit (one customer, one query, one seat). The question is whether serving each additional user makes or loses money.
Customer acquisition cost versus customer lifetime value. A healthy business earns much more from a customer than it spent to win them.
Churn is customers leaving. NRR over 100% means existing customers spend more each year, even after accounting for those who leave.
A multi-year contract to buy or reserve computing capacity (chips, cloud time, data-center power), often worth tens or hundreds of billions. Headlines often use the maximum "up to" value.
A headline maximum that depends on conditions. For example, part of Amazon's reported OpenAI investment was contingent on an IPO or a technical milestone.
A lasting advantage that stops competitors from copying a business and taking its customers.
A product built on top of someone else's AI model, adding interface, workflow or data. "Thin wrappers" add little and are easily copied, while "thick wrappers" become deep products.
The risk that a model provider releases your startup's main feature as a built-in capability.
AI products built for one industry (law, healthcare, accounting) with domain-specific workflows and data.
General-purpose tools used across industries, such as chat assistants or coding tools.
Charging per user per month, the classic software model.
Charging per amount used, such as per token, per API call or per credit.
Charging only when a result is achieved, such as per resolved customer-support ticket.
Selling the outcome of a service (bookkeeping done, tickets resolved) delivered largely by AI agents, instead of selling a tool to humans.
Large consulting firms (such as Accenture or Deloitte) that implement technology for enterprises. They are a major distribution channel for AI.
Everything involved in selling a product: sales, marketing, partnerships, customer success.
Customer-size segments: large corporations, medium firms, and small-and-medium businesses.
A small trial deployment to test whether AI works for a use case before full rollout.
When a product so clearly meets a market need that customers pull it from you.
Access to customers (channels, partnerships, existing user bases). In AI it is often a stronger moat than technology.
A loop in which usage generates data that improves the product, which attracts more usage.
How painful it is for a customer to move to a competitor.
The total revenue available if a product won every possible customer.
A for-profit company legally required to weigh a stated public mission alongside profit. Anthropic and OpenAI Group are PBCs.
A large general-purpose model trained on broad data. "Frontier" means among the most capable in existence.
A company training frontier models: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI and a few others.
Pretraining teaches a model general knowledge from huge datasets. Post-training (fine-tuning, reinforcement learning) shapes it into a helpful, safe assistant with particular skills.
Chips specialized for the parallel math AI needs. NVIDIA GPUs dominate, while Google TPUs and Amazon Trainium are alternatives.
CUDA is NVIDIA's programming platform for GPUs. A kernel is a small program that runs on the GPU, and writing faster kernels makes AI cheaper.
The practices and tools for deploying, monitoring and updating models in production reliably.
Human-written examples, ratings and expert demonstrations used to train and evaluate models. The work is often done by contractors via firms like Scale, Surge or Mercor.
Teams and systems that detect and prevent misuse of AI products.
How much a job's tasks could be done or assisted by AI. It is measured at the task level, not the job level.
Automation is AI doing the task instead of a person. Augmentation is AI helping a person do it better or faster.

An engineer embedded with a customer to build and deploy solutions on-site, half engineer and half consultant. The role originated at Palantir and became one of the fastest-growing AI roles in 2025–2026.

term: Solutions architect / Applied AI architect / solutions engineer
definition: Technical experts on the sales side who design how a customer will use the product, run demos and proofs of concept, and guide implementation.
A software engineer who builds products on top of foundation models (prompts, RAG, agents, evals), as distinct from training models.
An engineer who builds, trains, deploys and maintains machine-learning models in production.
Research engineers build the infrastructure and run large experiments. Research scientists set research direction and hypotheses. At frontier labs the line is blurry, and many postings are "RE/RS."
Makes training and inference faster and cheaper (kernels, compilers, parallelism).
Coordinates complex technical projects across teams, such as a data-center buildout or a model launch.
A salesperson who owns closing deals with a set of customers.
Sales compensation: base salary plus expected commission if targets are hit.
Ensures customers adopt and get value from a product after purchase, driving renewals and expansion.
Base salary + bonus + equity (stock) per year. Tech pay comparisons use TC.
Ownership granted as pay. It "vests" (becomes yours) over time, typically four years. At private labs its value depends on future valuations and liquidity.
Company-specific seniority ladders that determine pay bands.
A crowdsourced site where tech workers report verified compensation. It is the standard reference for tech pay, but skews toward large, high-paying companies.
Public evidence of what you can do: projects, write-ups, code repositories, demos. In AI it often matters more than credentials.
Deep expertise in one area (the vertical bar) plus broad working knowledge across many (the horizontal bar).
Time-boxed, paid programs where newcomers do research with mentorship. Examples are the Anthropic Fellows Program and MATS.
A domain expert (doctor, lawyer, coder, mathematician) paid to write, grade or critique model outputs for training and evaluation.
Government AI-safety bodies: the UK AI Security Institute and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation. They test frontier models and employ technical and policy staff.
The pattern of inflated expectations, disillusionment, then steady productive use that new technologies often follow.
Selling tools and infrastructure to everyone in a boom (as in the gold rush) instead of betting on one winner. NVIDIA is the classic AI example.
Tradespeople who run and maintain a data center's power and cooling systems 24/7.
Land with a confirmed connection to enough electricity, and the waiting list to connect new loads to the grid. Both are major bottlenecks for AI data centers.
